questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, which statement best describes withholding tax?

options.a: It is tax the recipient pays to the tax authority after receiving the gross amount
options.b: It is a separate final tax on the payer's own profits
options.c: It is a consumption tax added on top of the invoice amount, like VAT
options.d: It is tax deducted by the payer when a payment is made and credited as an advance payment against the recipient's income tax

questions.explanation: Withholding tax is a collection mechanism, not a separate tax: the payer acts as agent, deducts tax at the date of payment or settlement and remits it, and the recipient later uses the deduction as a credit against its final income tax. Option B wrongly treats it as a tax on the payer. Option A reverses the roles, and option C confuses it with VAT, which is added to the price rather than deducted from it.

questions.question: Under section 51(1) of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, where are the specific withholding tax rates found?

options.b: In regulations on deduction of tax at the time of payment, not in the text of the NTA 2025 or NTAA 2025
options.c: In circulars issued separately by each State Internal Revenue Service
options.d: In a rate table in the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 itself

questions.explanation: Section 51(1) NTAA 2025 requires the payer to deduct tax at the rate prescribed in regulations relating to deduction of tax, so the detailed rate table sits in subsidiary legislation. This lets rates be adjusted without amending the Acts. Option D is the tempting wrong choice, but neither 2025 Act contains the withholding rate table. Options A and C are not the legal home of the rates.

questions.question: Withholding tax regulations made under repealed laws, such as the 2024 Withholding Tax Regulations made under the old income tax Acts, still apply under the 2025 framework mainly because

options.a: the Nigeria Revenue Service re-issues them every year as a circular
options.b: the repealed Companies Income Tax Act remains in force until 2030
options.c: the savings provisions keep subsidiary legislation made under repealed Acts in force, so far as it is not inconsistent with the new Acts
options.d: regulations always survive the repeal of their parent Act, whatever the new law says

questions.explanation: When the 2025 Acts repealed the old income tax laws, savings provisions preserved existing subsidiary legislation to the extent it is consistent with the new Acts, which is why the existing withholding rates continue to apply. Option B is wrong because the old Acts were repealed. Option D overstates the position, since the regulations survive only because of the savings provisions and only where not inconsistent.

questions.question: Under the 2025 framework, a Nigerian company receives a dividend from another Nigerian company after 10% withholding tax has been deducted. How is the dividend treated in the recipient's hands?

options.a: As exempt income only if it is reinvested within one year
options.b: As franked investment income, which is not subject to further income tax
options.c: As a chargeable gain taxed at 30%
options.d: As part of its total profits, taxed again at 30% with credit for the withholding tax

questions.explanation: A dividend that has suffered withholding tax is franked investment income in the hands of a Nigerian company, so the withholding deduction is the final tax on it. Option D would tax the same dividend twice. Option C confuses dividends with gains on disposal of assets, and option A adds a condition that does not exist.

questions.question: Under section 105 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, a person who fails to deduct or withhold tax is liable to an administrative penalty of

options.a: N100,000 for the first month and N50,000 for each later month
options.c: 10% per annum of the amount not deducted

questions.explanation: Section 105 NTAA 2025 imposes an administrative penalty of 40% of the tax that should have been deducted, a strong deterrent aimed at the withholding agent. Option C is the rate for failing to remit tax that was deducted, which is a different offence. Option B reflects the old regime, and option A is the style of penalty used for late filing of returns.

questions.question: Under section 107(1) of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, a person who deducts tax but fails to remit it by the due date is liable to

options.b: interest at a fixed rate of 10% per annum only
options.c: an administrative penalty of 10% per annum of the tax not remitted, plus interest at the prevailing CBN monetary policy rate
options.d: a penalty of 40% of the tax not remitted, with no interest

questions.explanation: For tax deducted but not remitted, section 107(1) NTAA 2025 charges a penalty of 10% per annum on the unremitted amount plus interest at the prevailing CBN monetary policy rate, on top of the tax itself. Option D is the penalty for failing to deduct, not failing to remit. Option B is wrong because interest now follows the CBN monetary policy rate rather than a fixed rate.

questions.question: Under section 107(3) of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, a person convicted of failing to remit tax deducted is liable to a fine, imprisonment, or both. What is the maximum term of imprisonment?
questions.explanation: Section 107(3) NTAA 2025 provides for imprisonment of up to three years, a fine, or both on conviction for failure to remit tax deducted, because the agent is holding money that belongs to the government. Options D, B and C state terms that do not appear in the provision.

questions.question: Under section 41(2)(a) of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, within what period must a taxpayer deliver a notice of objection to a disputed assessment?

options.a: 90 days from the date of service
options.b: 14 days from the date of service
options.c: 30 days from the date of service of the notice of assessment
options.d: 12 months from the end of the year of assessment

questions.explanation: The objection must reach the relevant tax authority within 30 days of service of the disputed assessment, although the authority may extend the time for good cause. Option A is the time the tax authority has to respond, not the time to object. Options B and D are not the statutory period.

questions.question: Under section 41(6) of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, what happens if the tax authority does not respond to a valid notice of objection within the prescribed time?

options.a: Nothing; the authority may respond at any time
options.b: After 90 days without a response, the assessment becomes final and conclusive
options.c: After 90 days without a response, the taxpayer's objection is upheld
options.d: After 30 days without a response, the taxpayer must appeal to the Federal High Court

questions.explanation: The authority must respond within 90 days, and if it stays silent the taxpayer's objection is upheld, which protects taxpayers from indefinite delay. Option B reverses the consequence. Option D gives the wrong period and the wrong forum, and option A ignores the deadline.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, if the tax authority refuses a taxpayer's objection, what is the taxpayer's next step?

options.a: Appeal directly to the Supreme Court
options.b: Nothing; refusal of the objection is final
options.c: Appeal to the Tax Appeal Tribunal
options.d: Petition the National Assembly for a review

questions.explanation: A taxpayer whose objection is refused can exercise the right of appeal, starting at the Tax Appeal Tribunal, with further appeals on points of law going to the regular courts. Option A skips every step of the appeal ladder. Option D is not part of the dispute process, and option B is wrong because refusal opens the right of appeal.

questions.question: Coronet Engineering Ltd, a Nigerian resident company, makes payments in March 2026. Apply the withholding tax rates in force under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 and the 2024 Withholding Tax Regulations. It pays dividends of N60,000,000: N40,000,000 to corporate shareholders and N20,000,000 to individual shareholders, with withholding tax at 10% on both. What is the total withholding tax, and what net dividend do the shareholders receive?
questions.explanation: Dividends to both corporate and individual shareholders bear 10% withholding tax, so N60,000,000 x 10% = N6,000,000 is withheld and the shareholders receive N54,000,000. Option A wrongly withholds only on the corporate shareholders. Option C uses 5%, and option B uses 20%.

questions.question: Coronet Engineering Ltd, a Nigerian resident company, makes payments in March 2026. Apply the withholding tax rates in force under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 and the 2024 Withholding Tax Regulations. Coronet deducted withholding tax on dividends paid to corporate shareholders during March 2026. Under section 107(1) of the NTAA 2025, by what date must the tax be remitted?

options.c: 21 days after each dividend payment date

questions.explanation: Section 107(1) NTAA 2025 requires tax deducted to be remitted by the 21st day of the month after the month of deduction, so March deductions are due by 21 April 2026. Option C reflects the old 21-days-from-payment practice. Option B falls in the month of deduction itself, and option D is not the statutory date.

questions.question: Coronet Engineering Ltd, a Nigerian resident company, makes payments in March 2026. Apply the withholding tax rates in force under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 and the 2024 Withholding Tax Regulations. Prestige Insurance Plc pays Coronet professional fees of N9,000,000. The withholding tax rate on professional fees paid to a resident company is 5%. How much does Prestige deduct, and how much does Coronet receive?

options.a: Prestige deducts N180,000; Coronet receives N8,820,000
options.b: Prestige deducts N450,000; Coronet receives N8,550,000
options.c: Prestige deducts N900,000; Coronet receives N8,100,000
options.d: Prestige deducts N450,000; Coronet receives N9,000,000

questions.explanation: Prestige, as the payer, is the withholding agent: N9,000,000 x 5% = N450,000 is withheld and Coronet receives N8,550,000, using the N450,000 as a credit against its own tax. Option C applies the older 10% rate for resident companies. Option A uses the 2% rate for general services, and option D forgets that the tax comes out of the payment.

questions.question: Coronet Engineering Ltd, a Nigerian resident company, makes payments in March 2026. Apply the withholding tax rates in force under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 and the 2024 Withholding Tax Regulations. Coronet pays rent of N5,000,000 to a property company (withholding rate 10%) and N30,000,000 to Solo Builders Ltd, a resident company, for construction of a building (withholding rate 2%). What total withholding tax should Coronet deduct on these two payments?
questions.explanation: Each payment uses its own rate: rent N5,000,000 x 10% = N500,000 and building construction N30,000,000 x 2% = N600,000, giving N1,100,000. Option A applies 10% to both payments. Option C applies 5% to the construction payment, and option D leaves out the rent.

questions.question: Coronet Engineering Ltd, a Nigerian resident company, makes payments in March 2026. Apply the withholding tax rates in force under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 and the 2024 Withholding Tax Regulations. Coronet failed to deduct withholding tax at 10% on rent of N5,000,000 paid to a property company. What administrative penalty applies under section 105 of the NTAA 2025?
questions.explanation: The tax that should have been deducted is N5,000,000 x 10% = N500,000, and section 105 imposes a penalty of 40% of the amount not deducted, so 40% x N500,000 = N200,000, payable on top of the N500,000. Option D uses the old 10% penalty rate. Option A wrongly applies 40% to the rent itself, and option C is the tax, not the penalty.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 (NTAA), s.51, and the withholding regulations, Lekki Foods Ltd pays a dividend of N40,000,000 to its corporate shareholder, Orile Holdings Ltd. The WHT rate on dividends is 10%. How much WHT must Lekki Foods deduct?
questions.explanation: WHT = gross dividend x rate = N40,000,000 x 10% = N4,000,000, deducted by the paying company before the dividend is paid. Option C is the net dividend the shareholder actually receives, not the tax, while A and D apply rates that are not the dividend rate.

questions.question: Ikeja Paints Plc declares a dividend of N18,000,000 to its individual shareholders. Under the NTAA 2025 and the withholding regulations, WHT on dividends is 10%. What net amount will the shareholders receive in total?
questions.explanation: Net dividend = gross - WHT = N18,000,000 - (10% x N18,000,000) = N18,000,000 - N1,800,000 = N16,200,000. Option C is only the tax deducted, B ignores the deduction altogether, and A wrongly uses 5%.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025 and the withholding regulations, rent paid to a resident company attracts WHT at 10%. Surulere Logistics Ltd pays annual warehouse rent of N6,500,000 to Ojota Properties Ltd. How much WHT should Surulere Logistics deduct?
questions.explanation: WHT on rent = N6,500,000 x 10% = N650,000, and the tenant (the payer) deducts it when paying the rent. Options C and A use rates meant for other types of payment, such as professional fees and general services, so they understate the tax.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, professional fees paid to a resident company attract WHT at 5%. Marina Bank Plc pays legal fees of N9,000,000 to Adeyemi & Co Ltd, a resident company. How much WHT should the bank deduct?
questions.explanation: WHT = N9,000,000 x 5% = N450,000. Option C uses 10%, the higher rate that applies to non-resident recipients (and the rate many older examples used for residents), while D is the net fee paid after the deduction rather than the tax.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, consultancy and technical fees paid to a non-resident company attract WHT at 10%, which is the recipient's final tax. Apapa Refinery Ltd pays N20,000,000 to a German engineering firm for technical services. How much WHT should be deducted?
questions.explanation: WHT = N20,000,000 x 10% = N2,000,000, and for a non-resident company this deduction is the final Nigerian tax on that income. Option D applies the 5% resident rate, which is wrong because the higher rate exists precisely because the non-resident will not file a Nigerian return.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, supply of goods by a person other than the manufacturer or producer attracts WHT at 2%. Yaba Stores Ltd buys office furniture worth N15,000,000 from a resident trading company that did not make the furniture. How much WHT should Yaba Stores deduct?
questions.explanation: WHT = N15,000,000 x 2% = N300,000. The low 2% rate reflects the thin margins of traders. Option D wrongly applies the 7.5% VAT rate, and options C and B use rates for other payment types.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, construction of roads, bridges, buildings and power plants by a resident company attracts WHT at 2%, while other construction and related activities attract 5%. Ogun State pays Ibadan Builders Ltd N50,000,000 for building a bridge. How much WHT is deductible?
questions.explanation: Bridge building falls in the reduced 2% class, so WHT = N50,000,000 x 2% = N1,000,000. Option D uses the 5% rate for 'any other form of construction', which does not apply to roads, bridges, buildings or power plants.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, 'any other form of construction and related activities' (outside roads, bridges, buildings and power plants) carried out by a resident company attracts WHT at 5%. Ikoyi Towers Ltd pays N12,000,000 to a resident company for installing lifts and fire-escape systems. How much WHT should be deducted?
questions.explanation: Lift and fire-escape installation is construction-related work outside the 2% class, so WHT = N12,000,000 x 5% = N600,000. Option B applies the 2% rate meant only for roads, bridges, buildings and power plants, and D is the net payment, not the tax.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, directors' fees paid to a resident individual attract WHT at 15%. Sango Cement Plc pays a resident non-executive director fees of N4,000,000 for the year. How much WHT should the company deduct?
questions.explanation: WHT = N4,000,000 x 15% = N600,000; the 15% rate is set high to reflect the marginal personal income tax rate of directors. Option C uses the 20% rate that applies to non-resident directors.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, directors' fees paid to a non-resident individual attract WHT at 20%. Lagos Breweries Plc pays N5,000,000 in fees to a director who lives in the United Kingdom. How much WHT is deductible?
questions.explanation: WHT = N5,000,000 x 20% = N1,000,000. Option C uses the 15% resident-director rate, and B is the net fee remitted to the director, not the tax withheld.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, royalties paid to a resident individual attract WHT at 5% (the rate for corporate recipients is 10%). A publishing company pays royalties of N3,000,000 to a Nigerian author. How much WHT should be deducted?
questions.explanation: For an individual recipient, WHT on royalties = N3,000,000 x 5% = N150,000. Option A applies the 10% rate that applies when the royalty is paid to a company.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, commission paid to a resident company attracts WHT at 5%. An insurance company pays sales commission of N2,400,000 to Broad Street Agencies Ltd. How much WHT should be deducted?
questions.explanation: WHT = N2,400,000 x 5% = N120,000, since commission sits in the same 5% class as consultancy and professional fees for residents. Option D uses the non-resident rate, and A confuses WHT with the 7.5% VAT rate.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, professional fees paid to a resident attract WHT at 5%. Okafor Chambers, a resident partnership, invoices a client N7,200,000 (ignore VAT). How much cash will Okafor Chambers actually receive from the client?
questions.explanation: Cash received = fee - WHT = N7,200,000 - (5% x N7,200,000) = N7,200,000 - N360,000 = N6,840,000. Option A deducts 10% instead of 5%, C is just the WHT, and B ignores the deduction.

questions.question: A resident consultancy firm received a net payment of N9,500,000 after its client deducted WHT at 5% on its fee under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025. What was the gross fee before WHT?
questions.explanation: Gross = net / (1 - rate) = N9,500,000 / 0.95 = N10,000,000. Option C simply adds 5% to the net amount, which gives the wrong base because the 5% was taken from the gross figure, not from the net.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.105, a person who fails to deduct tax is liable to an administrative penalty of 40% of the amount not deducted. Oshodi Motors Ltd paid rent of N7,000,000 to a property company without deducting WHT at 10%. What is the administrative penalty?
questions.explanation: WHT not deducted = N7,000,000 x 10% = N700,000; penalty = 40% x N700,000 = N280,000. Option D wrongly applies 40% to the gross rent, and C adds the WHT itself to the penalty, which answers a different question (total liability).

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.105, failure to deduct tax attracts an administrative penalty of 40% of the amount not deducted, and the tax itself remains payable. Ajah Telecoms Ltd paid professional fees of N12,000,000 to a resident company without deducting WHT at 5%. What is the total of the WHT and the penalty now due (ignore interest)?
questions.explanation: WHT = N12,000,000 x 5% = N600,000; penalty = 40% x N600,000 = N240,000; total = N840,000. Option B uses a 10% WHT rate, A is the penalty alone, and C applies the 40% to the gross fee.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.107(1), deducted tax not remitted by the due date attracts an administrative penalty of 10% per annum. Badagry Farms Ltd deducted WHT of N3,650,000 and remitted it 60 days late. Time-apportion the penalty on a days/365 basis. What is the penalty (excluding interest)?
questions.explanation: Penalty = N3,650,000 x 10% x 60/365 = N60,000. Option C treats the 10% as a flat one-off charge instead of a per annum rate, and B uses the 40% rate that applies to failure to deduct, not failure to remit.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.107(1), interest at the prevailing CBN Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) is charged on deducted tax not remitted on time. Mushin Plastics Ltd remitted WHT of N2,000,000 73 days late when the MPR was 27% per annum. Using simple interest on a days/365 basis, what is the interest?
questions.explanation: Interest = N2,000,000 x 27% x 73/365 = N108,000. Option A charges a full year of interest, B uses the 10% penalty rate instead of the MPR, and D adds the penalty and interest together.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, Victoria Island Media Ltd made these payments to resident companies in April: office rent N4,000,000 (WHT 10%), legal fees N6,000,000 (WHT 5%), and stationery bought from a trading company (not the manufacturer) N10,000,000 (WHT 2%). What total WHT must it remit for April?
questions.explanation: Total = (N4,000,000 x 10%) + (N6,000,000 x 5%) + (N10,000,000 x 2%) = N400,000 + N300,000 + N200,000 = N900,000. Option D uses 10% on the legal fees, B wrongly applies a single 5% rate to every payment, and C uses 5% instead of 10% on the rent.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, fees paid to non-resident entertainers and sportspersons for performances in Nigeria attract WHT at 15%. A Lagos concert promoter pays a Ghanaian musician N8,000,000. How much WHT should be deducted?
questions.explanation: WHT = N8,000,000 x 15% = N1,200,000 on amounts earned in Nigeria by a non-resident entertainer. Option C uses the general 10% non-resident rate for fees, and B uses the non-resident directors' rate.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, compensation for loss of employment paid to an individual attracts WHT at 10%. Oyo Textiles Ltd pays a resident former manager compensation of N6,000,000. How much WHT should be deducted?
questions.explanation: WHT = N6,000,000 x 10% = N600,000. Option D is the net amount paid to the former employee, and B wrongly uses the resident directors' fee rate.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, winnings from lottery, gaming and reality shows paid to a resident individual attract WHT at 5%. A resident individual wins N2,000,000 in a licensed reality show. How much WHT should the organiser deduct?
questions.explanation: WHT = N2,000,000 x 5% = N100,000 for a resident winner. Option A applies the 15% rate that applies to a non-resident winner.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, co-location and telecommunication tower services attract WHT at 2% for resident recipients and 5% for non-resident recipients. A mobile network pays a resident tower company N25,000,000 for co-location. How much WHT should be deducted?
questions.explanation: WHT = N25,000,000 x 2% = N500,000, the reduced rate reflecting low industry margins. Option D applies the non-resident rate, and A confuses WHT with VAT.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, professional fees paid to a resident attract WHT at 5%, but where the recipient has no Tax Identification Number (TIN) the prescribed rate is doubled (capped at 20%). A client pays N8,000,000 in professional fees to a resident consultant who has no TIN. How much WHT should be deducted?
questions.explanation: With no TIN the 5% rate doubles to 10%, so WHT = N8,000,000 x 10% = N800,000. Option C ignores the no-TIN rule, while B jumps straight to the 20% cap, which only limits the doubled rate and is not itself the rate here.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, 'supply or rendering of services other than those specifically listed' attracts WHT at 2% for residents, and the rate is doubled where the supplier has no TIN. A company pays a resident cleaning contractor without a TIN N5,000,000. How much WHT should be deducted?
questions.explanation: The 2% general-services rate doubles to 4% for a supplier without a TIN: WHT = N5,000,000 x 4% = N200,000. Option C ignores the doubling, and B wrongly treats the 20% ceiling as the applicable rate.

questions.question: WHT deducted under the NTAA 2025, s.51, is an advance payment of the recipient's income tax, so it can be credited against the final liability. Agege Consulting Ltd's company income tax for the year is N9,000,000, and it holds valid WHT credit evidence of N2,500,000 for tax deducted by its clients. How much company income tax remains payable?
questions.explanation: Tax payable = final liability - WHT credits = N9,000,000 - N2,500,000 = N6,500,000. Option B ignores the credit, which would make the company pay the same tax twice, and C adds the credit instead of subtracting it.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.107(1), tax deducted at source must be remitted by the 21st day of the month immediately following the month of deduction. Ikorodu Steel Ltd deducted WHT in May 2026 and remitted it on 30 July 2026. Counting from the due date to the remittance date (excluding the due date), how many days late was the remittance?
questions.explanation: The May deduction was due by 21 June 2026, and 21 June to 30 July is 9 days in June plus 30 in July, which is 39 days. Option A counts from the end of May, and option B counts from 1 June instead of from the 21 June due date.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.107(1), WHT deducted must be remitted by the 21st day of the month immediately following the month of deduction. Kano Agro Ltd deducted WHT on payments made on 3 March 2026 and 28 March 2026. By what date must both deductions be remitted?
questions.explanation: All deductions made in a month share one deadline, the 21st of the next month, so both March deductions are due by 21 April 2026. Option B uses the old practice of counting 21 days from each payment date, which the NTAA replaced with a single monthly date.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, a resident company paying a resident professional firm deducts WHT at 5%. Ebute Metta Shipping Ltd pays a resident audit firm a fee of N4,000,000 and then fails to remit the deducted WHT for 146 days. The NTAA s.107(1) penalty is 10% per annum and interest is at the CBN MPR of 25% per annum, both time-apportioned on a days/365 basis. What is the total of penalty and interest (excluding the tax itself)?
questions.explanation: WHT = N4,000,000 x 5% = N200,000; penalty plus interest = N200,000 x (10% + 25%) x 146/365 = N28,000. Option C charges a full year, option D starts from a 10% WHT rate, and option B applies the rates to the gross fee instead of the tax.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 (NTAA), which description best fits withholding tax?

options.a: A separate tax charged on the payer's own profits at the time of payment
options.b: A consumption tax added to the price of every taxable supply
options.c: An advance payment of the recipient's income tax, deducted by the payer when a payment is made
options.d: A duty charged on written instruments that transfer property

questions.explanation: Withholding tax is not a standalone tax: it is part of the payee's eventual income tax collected early by the payer. Option A wrongly makes the payer the taxpayer, B describes VAT, and D describes stamp duty.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.51, the 'withholding agent' in withholding tax is the:

options.a: Tax Appeal Tribunal that settles disputes
options.b: Recipient, who pays the tax when filing returns
options.c: Bank through which the payment passes
options.d: Payer, who deducts the tax from the payment and remits it

questions.explanation: The payer (for example, the company paying rent or fees) is the agent who deducts the tax at the date of payment or settlement and remits it to the tax authority. Option B describes the person who suffers the deduction, not the agent.

questions.question: Which section of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 is the core provision on deduction of tax at source (withholding tax)?
questions.explanation: Section 51 requires a person making a payment to deduct tax at the rate prescribed in the withholding regulations. Option D is the VAT revenue-distribution section, B is the penalty for failure to deduct, and A deals with VAT returns.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 (NTAA) framework, where are the specific withholding tax rates (for example, 10% on rent) found?

options.a: In a table inside the NTAA 2025 penalty provisions
options.b: In regulations on deduction of tax at source, to which NTAA 2025 s.51 refers
options.c: In the First Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025
options.d: In the Ninth Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025

questions.explanation: Section 51 of the NTAA says tax is deducted 'at the rate prescribed in regulations', so the rate tables live in subsidiary legislation, currently the 2024 withholding regulations. Option D is the stamp duty rate schedule, and C deals with capital allowances.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.107(1), by when must tax deducted at source be remitted?

options.a: By the 14th day of the month following the end of the quarter
options.c: Within 30 days of the end of the accounting year
options.d: By the 21st day of the month immediately following the month of deduction

questions.explanation: Section 107(1) sets one monthly deadline: the 21st day of the month after the deduction. Option B is the older practice of counting 21 days from each payment, which the new Act replaced with a fixed date.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.105, what is the administrative penalty for failing to deduct or withhold tax?
questions.explanation: Section 105 imposes an administrative penalty of 40% of the tax that should have been deducted. Option C was the old CITA-era rate, and D wrongly applies the 40% to the whole payment instead of to the tax.

questions.question: A company paid a supplier without deducting WHT, while another company deducted WHT but kept the money for three months. Under the NTAA 2025, which statement correctly matches each failure to its penalty?

options.a: Failure to deduct: 10% per annum (s.107); failure to remit: 40% of the tax (s.105)
options.b: Failure to deduct: 40% of the amount not deducted (s.105); failure to remit: 10% per annum plus CBN MPR interest (s.107)
options.c: Both failures: 10% per annum plus MPR interest (s.107)
options.d: Both failures: 40% of the tax plus MPR interest (s.105)

questions.explanation: The NTAA treats the two failures separately: not deducting attracts 40% of the undeducted tax under s.105, while deducting but not remitting attracts 10% per annum plus interest at the MPR under s.107. Option A swaps the two, and options D and C wrongly use one rule for both.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.107(3), on conviction for failure to remit tax deducted, an offender is liable to:

options.a: Imprisonment of up to ten years and forfeiture of business assets
options.b: Imprisonment of up to three years, a fine of not less than the principal plus up to 50% of it, or both
options.c: Imprisonment of up to six months only
options.d: A fine equal to 10% of the tax with no imprisonment

questions.explanation: Beyond the administrative penalty, s.107(3) creates a criminal sanction of up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of not less than the principal amount plus a penalty of up to 50% of it. The other options state terms that are not in the provision.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.41, Bodija Traders Ltd objected to a WHT assessment, but the tax authority sent no response within 90 days. What is the legal effect?

options.a: The objection lapses and must be refiled
options.b: The matter goes automatically to the Supreme Court
options.c: The assessment becomes final and conclusive
options.d: The taxpayer's objection is treated as upheld

questions.explanation: Section 41 requires the authority to respond within 90 days, 'otherwise the objection of the taxpayer shall be upheld'. Option C reverses the rule by favouring the authority's silence, and the appeal route in B starts at the Tax Appeal Tribunal, not the Supreme Court.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025 and the withholding regulations, for a non-resident company that earns professional, consultancy or management fees from Nigeria, WHT deducted under the 2025 framework is best described as:

options.a: A refundable deposit returned on request
options.b: An advance tax to be offset in a Nigerian CIT return
options.c: A final tax on that income
options.d: A deduction that only applies if the company registers in Nigeria

questions.explanation: For non-residents, WHT on such fees earned from Nigeria is the final tax, which is why the non-resident rate (10%) is higher than the resident rate (5%). Option B describes how WHT works for a resident company, which files a return and claims credit.

questions.question: A Nigerian company receives a dividend from another Nigerian company after 10% WHT has been deducted. Under the NTAA 2025, this dividend is called 'franked investment income'. What does that mean?

options.a: It is not subject to further income tax in the hands of the receiving company
options.b: It is exempt from WHT at the time of payment
options.c: It is taxed again at 30% in the receiving company
options.d: It must be grossed up and taxed at the development levy rate

questions.explanation: Franked investment income is a dividend that has already borne WHT, so it is not charged to further income tax in the recipient company. Option B is wrong because WHT is in fact deducted when the dividend is paid; that deduction is what 'franks' it.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.51, at what point must the payer deduct WHT?

options.a: When the recipient files its annual return
options.b: Only when the tax authority issues a demand notice
options.c: At the date of payment or settlement of the amount
options.d: At the end of the payer's financial year

questions.explanation: Section 51 of the NTAA requires deduction at the time the amount is paid or settled, and the withholding regulations treat the earlier of payment or settlement as the trigger. Options A and D would delay collection, which defeats the purpose of deduction at the point of payment.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of withholding tax under the NTAA 2025 framework?

options.a: The rates are set in regulations rather than in the Acts
options.b: It is a final tax for resident companies on all their income
options.c: The payer acts as agent for the tax authority
options.d: It is credited against the resident recipient's final income tax

questions.explanation: For a resident company, WHT is only an advance payment that is credited against its final income tax, so it is not a final tax for them. Options C, D and A are all genuine features of the system.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, which payment to a RESIDENT INDIVIDUAL attracts the highest WHT rate?
questions.explanation: Directors' fees paid to a resident individual attract 15%, the highest of the four. Dividends and rent (B, A) attract 10%, and professional fees (C) attract 5%.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, supply of goods 'other than by the manufacturer or producer' attracts WHT at 2%. Ijebu Bottling Ltd buys glass bottles directly from the factory that makes them. What WHT applies to the purchase price?

options.a: 10%, because the buyer is a company
options.b: 2%, as on any supply of goods
options.d: No WHT, because the goods are bought directly from the manufacturer

questions.explanation: The 2% class covers only goods supplied by someone other than the manufacturer or producer, such as traders. A purchase straight from the factory falls outside it, so option B overlooks the key qualification in the rule.

questions.question: Under the 2024 withholding regulations applied with the NTAA 2025, Ketu Bakery Ltd, a small company, buys flour worth N1,500,000 in a month from a trader who has a valid TIN. Its total purchases from that trader that month are below N2,000,000. What is Ketu Bakery's WHT obligation on this purchase?

options.b: Deduct 5% because the supplier is a trader
options.c: Deduct 2% and remit by the 21st of the next month
options.d: Deduct 4% because the buyer is a small company

questions.explanation: The regulations relieve a small company from deducting WHT where its transactions with a supplier do not exceed N2,000,000 in a month and the supplier has a valid TIN. Option C applies the normal 2% supply-of-goods rule, which this relief displaces.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, to which authority should a company remit WHT deducted from rent paid to another COMPANY?

options.b: The State Internal Revenue Service of the landlord's state

questions.explanation: The NRS, which replaced FIRS, administers WHT where the recipient is a company or a non-resident. WHT deducted from individuals goes to the relevant State IRS (option B), and the JRB (D) coordinates rather than collects.

questions.question: Compared with the old CITA regime, how did the NTAA 2025 change the penalty for failure to deduct WHT?

options.a: It was replaced by a fixed fine of N50,000
options.b: It fell from 40% to 10% of the amount not deducted
options.c: It rose from 10% to 40% of the amount not deducted
options.d: It stayed at 10% but interest was removed

questions.explanation: The old CITA penalty for failure to deduct was 10% of the amount not deducted; NTAA s.105 raised it to 40%, a much stronger deterrent. Option B reverses the direction of the change.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, interest on late remittance of deducted tax is charged at:

options.b: The prevailing CBN Monetary Policy Rate
options.c: The commercial bank prime lending rate
options.d: A fixed 10% per annum, as under the old CITA

questions.explanation: The NTAA links interest to the prevailing CBN Monetary Policy Rate, so it moves with monetary policy. Option D is the fixed rate used under the repealed law, which is a common mix-up.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, why is the WHT rate on consultancy fees higher for a non-resident company (10%) than for a resident company (5%)?

options.a: Because for the non-resident the deduction is its final Nigerian tax
options.b: Because residents receive a 50% statutory discount
options.c: Because the rate includes VAT on imported services
options.d: Because non-residents are charged a penalty for not registering

questions.explanation: The higher non-resident rate exists because the deduction is the final tax for a non-resident that does not file a Nigerian return. Option C confuses WHT with VAT, and the other options describe rules that do not exist.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, what happens to the WHT rate where a supplier (other than for passive income such as dividends) does not have a Tax Identification Number?

options.a: The prescribed rate is doubled, subject to a maximum of 20%
options.c: The rate is halved to encourage registration
options.d: WHT is not deducted until the supplier registers

questions.explanation: Suppliers without a TIN suffer twice the prescribed rate, capped at 20%, which pushes businesses to register. Option B confuses this with the 40% penalty for failure to deduct.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.51, Bariga Consulting Ltd suffered WHT of N1,200,000 on fees from several clients during the year. How does this WHT affect Bariga's own company income tax?

options.a: Bariga can deduct the WHT as an expense in arriving at profit
options.b: Bariga must pay the N1,200,000 again with its CIT
options.c: Bariga can use the WHT, supported by credit evidence, to reduce its final CIT payable
options.d: The WHT is lost because it was paid by the clients

questions.explanation: Because WHT is an advance payment of the recipient's income tax, Bariga sets the amount off against its CIT liability. Option B would tax the same income twice, and A treats a tax credit as a business expense, which it is not.

questions.question: Under the withholding regulations applied by the NTAA 2025, which of these payments to a RESIDENT company does NOT attract WHT at 10%?
questions.explanation: Management fees fall in the commission, consultancy, technical, management and professional fees class, which is 5% for residents. Dividends, interest and rent (options C, A, D) all attract 10%.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, what is the main difference between an exempt supply (s.185) and a zero-rated supply (s.186)?

options.a: Neither carries output VAT, but input VAT on a zero-rated supply is recoverable while input VAT on an exempt supply is not
options.b: Zero-rated supplies are charged at 7.5% and refunded later
options.c: Exempt supplies allow input VAT recovery while zero-rated supplies do not
options.d: There is no practical difference; both terms mean the supply is outside VAT

questions.explanation: Both exempt and zero-rated supplies leave the customer paying no VAT, but only a zero-rated supplier can recover the input VAT on its purchases; for an exempt supplier, input VAT becomes a cost. Option C reverses the rule. Option D misses this input VAT difference, which is exactly why the distinction matters.

questions.question: A Nigerian software company sells its services only to clients abroad. Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, exported services are zero-rated. What is the commercial effect for the company?

options.a: It cannot recover any input VAT, so VAT becomes a cost of the business
options.b: It must charge its foreign clients 7.5% VAT and claim a refund later
options.c: It is automatically exempt from company income tax on its export profits
options.d: It charges 0% VAT to its foreign clients and can still recover the input VAT it pays on its own purchases

questions.explanation: Zero-rating means the export is taxed at 0%, so the foreign client pays no Nigerian VAT, while the company can claim back the input VAT on things like equipment and services, keeping its prices competitive. Option A describes an exempt supplier, not a zero-rated one. Option C is wrong because VAT zero-rating does not affect company income tax.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, which of the following is an exempt supply rather than a zero-rated supply?
questions.explanation: Land and buildings are listed among exempt supplies, so no VAT is charged and the supplier cannot recover related input VAT. Options A, D and C are all zero-rated under the 2025 Act, which means 0% VAT with input VAT still recoverable.

questions.question: Under section 81(1) of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, how is net VAT revenue shared among the tiers of government?

options.a: 85% Federal Government, 15% States and FCT, 0% Local Governments
options.b: 15% Federal Government, 50% States and FCT, 35% Local Governments
options.c: 10% Federal Government, 55% States and FCT, 35% Local Governments
options.d: 50% Federal Government, 30% States and FCT, 20% Local Governments

questions.explanation: Section 81(1) NTAA 2025 gives 10% to the Federal Government, 55% to the States and FCT and 35% to Local Governments, shifting more VAT to sub-national governments. Option B was the sharing ratio under the repealed VAT Act. Options D and A are not the statutory ratio.

questions.question: Under section 81(2) of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, on what basis is the VAT share of States and Local Governments distributed among them?

options.a: 100% by the place where VAT returns are filed
options.b: 50% by population, 30% equally and 20% by derivation of returns filed
options.c: 50% equally, 20% by population and 30% by consumption
options.d: Equally among all States and Local Governments

questions.explanation: The sub-national share is split 50% equally, 20% by population and 30% by consumption, so states where goods and services are actually consumed get a bigger share. Option B reshuffles the figures and wrongly uses where returns are filed. Option A ignores the equality and population parts, and option D ignores population and consumption.

questions.question: Under section 81(3) of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, how is 'consumption' determined for the 30% consumption part of VAT distribution?

options.a: By each state's share of the national population
options.b: By the number of VAT-registered businesses in each state
options.c: By the state where the supplier's head office files its VAT returns
options.d: By the place where the goods or services are consumed, irrespective of where the VAT return is filed

questions.explanation: Consumption is measured by where the goods or services are actually consumed, not where the return is filed, so a company with a Lagos head office cannot pull all the consumption share into Lagos. Option C is exactly what the provision rules out. Option A is the separate population factor, and option B is not a factor.

questions.question: Radiance Health Ltd, a VAT-registered company, has these transactions for a month in 2026 under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 (standard rate 7.5%): sales of taxable medical devices N25,000,000 (VAT-exclusive); zero-rated sales of medical equipment N8,000,000; purchases of taxable components N10,000,000 (VAT-exclusive); purchases of zero-rated medicines N4,000,000; import of machinery with a CIF value of N6,000,000, on which import VAT at 7.5% of CIF was paid; and consultancy services bought for N2,140,000 (VAT-inclusive). All inputs relate to its taxable and zero-rated supplies. Round to the nearest naira. What is Radiance's output VAT for the month?
questions.explanation: Output VAT arises only on the taxable sales: N25,000,000 x 7.5% = N1,875,000, while the zero-rated sales carry VAT at 0%. Option B wrongly charges 7.5% on the zero-rated sales as well. Option D treats the VAT-exclusive figure as VAT-inclusive, and option A is the input VAT figure.

questions.question: Radiance Health Ltd, a VAT-registered company, has these transactions for a month in 2026 under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 (standard rate 7.5%): sales of taxable medical devices N25,000,000 (VAT-exclusive); zero-rated sales of medical equipment N8,000,000; purchases of taxable components N10,000,000 (VAT-exclusive); purchases of zero-rated medicines N4,000,000; import of machinery with a CIF value of N6,000,000, on which import VAT at 7.5% of CIF was paid; and consultancy services bought for N2,140,000 (VAT-inclusive). All inputs relate to its taxable and zero-rated supplies. Round to the nearest naira. What is Radiance's recoverable input VAT for the month?
questions.explanation: Recoverable input VAT is N750,000 on components (N10,000,000 x 7.5%), N450,000 on the imported machinery (N6,000,000 x 7.5%) and N149,302 on the consultancy (N2,140,000 x 7.5/107.5), a total of N1,349,302. The 2025 Act allows input VAT on services and fixed assets used for taxable or zero-rated supplies. Option C leaves out the consultancy, option A wrongly adds VAT on zero-rated medicines that carried no VAT, and option D applies 7.5% to a VAT-inclusive amount.

questions.question: Radiance Health Ltd, a VAT-registered company, has these transactions for a month in 2026 under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 (standard rate 7.5%): sales of taxable medical devices N25,000,000 (VAT-exclusive); zero-rated sales of medical equipment N8,000,000; purchases of taxable components N10,000,000 (VAT-exclusive); purchases of zero-rated medicines N4,000,000; import of machinery with a CIF value of N6,000,000, on which import VAT at 7.5% of CIF was paid; and consultancy services bought for N2,140,000 (VAT-inclusive). All inputs relate to its taxable and zero-rated supplies. Round to the nearest naira. What is Radiance's net VAT position for the month?
questions.explanation: Net VAT is output VAT less recoverable input VAT: N1,875,000 - N1,349,302 = N525,698, and because output exceeds input it is payable to the NRS. Option C gets the direction wrong. Option A leaves out the input VAT on the consultancy, and option B ignores input VAT altogether.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, by when must a monthly VAT return be filed, and if a taxpayer is in a refund position, within what time must the NRS refund the tax after a valid refund request?

options.a: By the 14th day of the following month; within 90 days
options.b: By the 30th day of the following month; within 12 months
options.c: By the 21st day of the following month; within 30 days of a valid request
options.d: By the 21st day of the following month; within 90 days

questions.explanation: Section 22(1) NTAA 2025 requires the VAT return by the 21st day of the following month, and section 56(3) requires the NRS to refund, or allow a set-off, within 30 days of a valid refund request. Option D is tempting because 90 days applies to general (non-VAT) refunds, but VAT refunds have the shorter 30-day timeline. Option B confuses the refund period with the 12 months a taxpayer has to make the request.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 (NTA), s.147, VAT is charged at 7.5%. Ikeja Furniture Ltd sells taxable goods for N18,000,000 (VAT-exclusive). What output VAT should it charge?
questions.explanation: Output VAT = VAT-exclusive price x 7.5% = N18,000,000 x 7.5% = N1,350,000. Option A wrongly applies the 7.5/107.5 fraction, which is only for VAT-inclusive prices, and D is the total invoice value including VAT.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.147, VAT is 7.5%. Ajegunle Electronics Ltd's sales for the month were N21,500,000, VAT-INCLUSIVE. What is the output VAT contained in this figure?
questions.explanation: For a VAT-inclusive amount, VAT = inclusive price x 7.5/107.5 = N21,500,000 x 7.5/107.5 = N1,500,000. Option A multiplies the inclusive figure by 7.5%, which charges VAT on VAT, and B is the VAT-exclusive sales value.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, VAT is charged at 7.5%. A customer paid a VAT-inclusive price of N4,300,000 for a generator. What was the VAT-exclusive price?
questions.explanation: VAT-exclusive price = inclusive price / 1.075 = N4,300,000 / 1.075 = N4,000,000. Option B deducts 7.5% of the inclusive price, which takes out too much because the 7.5% was calculated on the smaller exclusive figure.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, ss.147 and 155, VAT is 7.5% and input VAT is credited against output VAT. In June, Owerri Packaging Ltd made taxable sales of N30,000,000 and taxable purchases of N12,000,000 (both VAT-exclusive), all used for its taxable supplies. What is the net VAT payable?
questions.explanation: Net VAT = output VAT - input VAT = (N30,000,000 x 7.5%) - (N12,000,000 x 7.5%) = N2,250,000 - N900,000 = N1,350,000. Option A ignores the input VAT credit, and C adds input VAT instead of deducting it.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, VAT at 7.5% is collected at each stage of a supply chain, with input VAT credited. A manufacturer sells detergent to a wholesaler for N4,000,000, the wholesaler sells it to a retailer for N6,000,000, and the retailer sells it to consumers for N9,000,000 (all VAT-exclusive). How much net VAT does the RETAILER remit?
questions.explanation: Retailer's net VAT = output - input = (N9,000,000 - N6,000,000) x 7.5% = N225,000. Option C ignores the retailer's input VAT credit, and B adds up VAT at every stage as if there were no credit mechanism.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, VAT at 7.5% is collected at each stage of a supply chain with credit for input VAT. Cement passes from a manufacturer (sale price N5,000,000) to a distributor (sale price N8,000,000) to a retailer (sale price N12,000,000), all VAT-exclusive. What TOTAL VAT reaches the NRS from the whole chain?
questions.explanation: With input credits, total VAT remitted equals 7.5% of the final selling price: N12,000,000 x 7.5% = N900,000 (that is N375,000 + N225,000 + N300,000). Option C sums output VAT at each stage, which ignores the credits, and that cascading result is what the old sales tax produced.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, VAT is 7.5% on taxable supplies and exported goods (other than oil and gas) are zero-rated under s.186, with input VAT recoverable. In May, Calabar Cashew Ltd made local taxable sales of N10,000,000 and zero-rated exports of N6,000,000; its taxable purchases were N9,000,000 (all VAT-exclusive, all used in making these supplies). What is its net VAT payable?
questions.explanation: Output VAT = N10,000,000 x 7.5% = N750,000 (exports at 0%); input VAT = N9,000,000 x 7.5% = N675,000, all recoverable because zero-rated supplies keep the right to input credit; net = N75,000. Option A wrongly charges VAT on the exports, and D disallows the input VAT linked to the exports as if they were exempt.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.186, exported services are zero-rated, so the supplier charges 0% but can recover input VAT. Yaba Code Ltd's only supplies in a quarter were exported software services of N40,000,000. It paid VAT at 7.5% on taxable purchases of N8,000,000 (VAT-exclusive). What is its VAT refund position?

options.d: Nil, because exports carry no VAT

questions.explanation: Output VAT on zero-rated exports is nil, while input VAT = N8,000,000 x 7.5% = N600,000, so Yaba Code is owed a refund or credit of N600,000. Option B wrongly charges 7.5% on the exports, and option C nets that wrong output VAT against the input VAT; option D treats the exports as exempt, which would give no recovery.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, VAT is 7.5% and input VAT on purchases used to make EXEMPT supplies cannot be recovered. Lekki Land Developers Ltd sells only land and buildings (exempt under s.185) and buys taxable building services of N6,000,000 (VAT-exclusive). What is the total cost of these services to the company, including VAT?
questions.explanation: An exempt supplier cannot reclaim input VAT, so the VAT becomes part of its cost: N6,000,000 + (7.5% x N6,000,000) = N6,450,000. Option A assumes the VAT is recoverable, which is only true for taxable or zero-rated suppliers.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.149, VAT on imported goods is charged on a value that includes customs duty. Ibadan Pharma Ltd imports machinery with a CIF value of N20,000,000; import duty is 10% of CIF. Ignoring other levies, what import VAT at 7.5% is payable on CIF plus duty?
questions.explanation: VAT base = CIF + duty = N20,000,000 + N2,000,000 = N22,000,000; VAT = N22,000,000 x 7.5% = N1,650,000. Option B charges VAT on CIF alone and forgets to add the duty, the most common slip.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.149, import VAT is charged on CIF plus import duty. Nnewi Parts Ltd imports spare parts with a CIF value of USD 50,000 when USD 1 = N1,500. Import duty is 20% of CIF. Ignoring other levies, what is the import VAT at 7.5%?
questions.explanation: CIF = 50,000 x N1,500 = N75,000,000; duty = 20% = N15,000,000; VAT = (N75,000,000 + N15,000,000) x 7.5% = N6,750,000. Option A omits the duty from the base, and D uses the old 5% VAT rate.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.81(1), net VAT revenue is shared 10% to the Federal Government, 55% to the States and FCT, and 35% to Local Governments. If net VAT revenue for a month is N800 billion, what is the share of the States and FCT?
questions.explanation: States and FCT share = 55% x N800 billion = N440 billion. Option C uses the 50% share under the repealed VAT Act, while D and A are the Local Government and Federal Government shares.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.81(1), net VAT revenue is shared 10% Federal Government, 55% States and FCT, and 35% Local Governments. If net VAT revenue is N1,200 billion, what goes to Local Governments?
questions.explanation: Local Governments receive 35% x N1,200 billion = N420 billion. Option C is the States' 55% share, and D uses the 15% Federal share under the old law.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.81(1), the Federal Government receives 10% of net VAT revenue. Under the repealed VAT Act it received 15%. If net VAT revenue is N600 billion, how much does the Federal Government receive under the NTAA 2025?
questions.explanation: Federal share = 10% x N600 billion = N60 billion. Option D applies the old 15% share, which the NTAA reduced so that States and Local Governments receive more.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.81(2), the VAT share of the States and FCT is distributed 50% equally, 20% on population and 30% on consumption. If the States and FCT pool for a month is N550 billion, how much is distributed on the basis of POPULATION?
questions.explanation: Population portion = 20% x N550 billion = N110 billion. Option A is the 30% consumption portion, and D is the 50% shared equally.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.81(2), VAT shared among Local Governments is distributed 50% equally, 20% on population and 30% on consumption, where consumption is determined by the place of consumption. If the Local Government pool is N350 billion, how much is distributed on the basis of CONSUMPTION?
questions.explanation: Consumption portion = 30% x N350 billion = N105 billion. Option B is the 20% population portion, and C wrongly reuses the 35% Local Government share of the national pool.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.101, a taxable person who fails to file a return is liable to N100,000 for the first month of failure and N50,000 for each subsequent month. Onitsha Traders Ltd filed its VAT return three months late. What is the penalty?
questions.explanation: Penalty = N100,000 (first month) + 2 x N50,000 (second and third months) = N200,000. Option B charges N100,000 for every month, and A counts three subsequent months instead of two.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.100, a person who fails to register is liable to N50,000 for the first month of failure and N25,000 for each subsequent month. Ajao Imports Ltd delayed its registration by four months. What is the penalty?
questions.explanation: Penalty = N50,000 (first month) + 3 x N25,000 = N125,000. Option C charges N50,000 for all four months, and B counts four subsequent months instead of three.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.107(1), VAT collected but not remitted on time attracts an administrative penalty of 10% per annum plus interest at the CBN MPR. Warri Gas Services Ltd remitted VAT of N2,920,000 50 days late when the MPR was 27%. Time-apportioning both on a days/365 basis, what is the total of penalty and interest?
questions.explanation: Penalty + interest = N2,920,000 x (10% + 27%) x 50/365 = N148,000. Option B treats the 10% as a flat charge, A leaves out the penalty, and D applies the 40% failure-to-deduct rate.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, input VAT on services used for taxable supplies is recoverable. Port Harcourt Logistics Ltd paid a VAT-INCLUSIVE consultancy fee of N2,150,000 (VAT at 7.5%) for its taxable business. How much input VAT can it claim?
questions.explanation: Input VAT = N2,150,000 x 7.5/107.5 = N150,000. Option C applies 7.5% to the VAT-inclusive figure, which overstates the claim, and B is the VAT-exclusive fee.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025 (VAT 7.5%; zero-rated exports under s.186; import VAT on CIF plus duty under s.149), Aba Leather Ltd had these July figures: local taxable sales N32,250,000 (VAT-INCLUSIVE); exports N5,000,000 (zero-rated); taxable purchases N14,000,000 (VAT-exclusive); purchases from an exempt supplier N2,000,000; and imported machinery with CIF N6,000,000 and 5% import duty. What is the net VAT payable?
questions.explanation: Output VAT = N32,250,000 x 7.5/107.5 = N2,250,000; input VAT = (N14,000,000 x 7.5%) + (N6,300,000 x 7.5%) = N1,050,000 + N472,500 = N1,522,500; net payable = N727,500. Option B takes 7.5% of the VAT-inclusive sales, A wrongly claims input VAT on the exempt purchases, and C charges VAT on the zero-rated exports.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.155, net VAT is output VAT minus input VAT. Kaduna Mills Ltd's output VAT for August was N900,000 and its net VAT payable was N270,000. How much input VAT did it claim?
questions.explanation: Input VAT = output VAT - net VAT payable = N900,000 - N270,000 = N630,000. Option D adds the two figures instead of subtracting them.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, input VAT on a cost used for both taxable and exempt supplies must be apportioned. Jos Dairy Ltd paid input VAT of N600,000 on a shared factory overhead. Taxable supplies are 75% of its total supplies and exempt supplies 25%. Apportioning by this ratio, how much input VAT can it recover?
questions.explanation: Recoverable input VAT = N600,000 x 75% = N450,000; the 25% linked to exempt supplies is a cost. Option B recovers everything, and D wrongly applies the 7.5% rate a second time to an amount that is already VAT.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, the final consumer bears the economic burden of VAT at 7.5%. A consumer pays N10,750,000, VAT-inclusive, for a car from a dealer. How much of this payment is VAT?
questions.explanation: VAT = N10,750,000 x 7.5/107.5 = N750,000. Option C multiplies the inclusive price by 7.5%, and B applies the old 5% rate to the inclusive price.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, VAT at 7.5% is a multi-stage tax with credit for input VAT. A distributor buys bottled water for N5,000,000 and sells it for N7,000,000 (both VAT-exclusive). What net VAT does the distributor remit?
questions.explanation: Net VAT = (N7,000,000 - N5,000,000) x 7.5% = N150,000, which is VAT on the value the distributor adds. Option A is its output VAT before the input credit, and C is only its input VAT.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, baby products are exempt under s.185 and other goods are taxable at 7.5%. Ikotun Supermarket Ltd sold N12,000,000 of goods (VAT-exclusive) in a month, of which N3,000,000 were baby products. What output VAT should it account for?
questions.explanation: Only the N9,000,000 of taxable goods bear VAT: N9,000,000 x 7.5% = N675,000. Option C wrongly charges VAT on the exempt baby products as well.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, basic food items are zero-rated under s.186 and other goods are taxable at 7.5%. Ilorin Foods Ltd sold taxable goods of N20,000,000 and basic food items of N8,000,000. It made taxable purchases of N10,000,000 for its taxable goods and N4,000,000 for its food items (all VAT-exclusive). What is its net VAT payable?
questions.explanation: Output VAT = N20,000,000 x 7.5% = N1,500,000; input VAT = (N10,000,000 + N4,000,000) x 7.5% = N1,050,000, all recoverable because zero-rated supplies keep input credit; net = N450,000. Option B disallows the input VAT on the food side as if those sales were exempt, and D charges VAT on the zero-rated food.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.56, the NRS must refund VAT not later than 30 days after receiving a valid refund request. Abeokuta Exporters Ltd's valid request was received by the NRS on 10 March 2026. By what date must the refund (or set-off) be made?
questions.explanation: Thirty days from 10 March 2026 is 9 April 2026. Option D applies the 90-day period that governs general (non-VAT) tax refunds under s.55, and A confuses the refund deadline with the monthly filing date.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.22(1), a VAT return is due on or before the 21st day of the month following the month of the transactions. Benin Rubber Ltd's transactions took place in November 2026. When is its VAT return due?
questions.explanation: November returns are due by 21 December 2026, the 21st day of the following month. Option D skips a month, and C uses a 14th-day date that is not the filing deadline for a taxable person's own return.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, land and buildings, including interests in them, are exempt from VAT under s.185. Ilupeju Estates Ltd receives annual rent of N12,000,000 from a commercial tenant. What VAT should it charge on the rent?
questions.explanation: Rent is a supply of an interest in land or buildings, which is exempt, so no VAT is charged. Option C wrongly treats the rent as a standard taxable supply.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, VAT is 7.5%. A non-resident streaming company supplies services to Nigerian subscribers worth N6,000,000 (VAT-exclusive) in a month. Under s.150 it must charge Nigerian VAT on these supplies. How much VAT is due?

options.a: Nil, because the supplier is non-resident

questions.explanation: Services provided to and consumed by persons in Nigeria are taxable even if the supplier is abroad: VAT = N6,000,000 x 7.5% = N450,000. Option A assumes foreign suppliers are outside the Nigerian VAT net, which s.150 rejects.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, s.147, what is the standard rate of VAT on taxable supplies?
questions.explanation: Section 147 charges VAT at 7.5% on the value of all taxable supplies, the same rate set by the Finance Act 2019. Option A is the pre-2020 rate under the old VAT Act.

questions.question: A tax on consumption, collected at every stage of the supply chain, where each registered person charges tax on sales and deducts tax paid on purchases, and the final consumer bears the burden. Under the NTA 2025, this is:
questions.explanation: This is VAT: a multi-stage consumption tax with an input credit mechanism, so the full burden ends up on the final consumer. Option C is an advance income tax deducted by payers, and D is a single-stage charge on locally made goods.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, 'input VAT' means:

options.a: VAT paid by a taxable person to a supplier on taxable supplies made to that person
options.b: VAT collected by government agencies on contracts
options.c: VAT paid by the final consumer only
options.d: VAT charged by a taxable person on supplies it makes

questions.explanation: Input VAT is the VAT a business pays on its purchases, which it can credit against its output VAT. Option D is the definition of output VAT.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, 'output VAT' means:

options.a: VAT charged and collected by a taxable person on the taxable supplies it makes
options.b: VAT paid on goods imported into Nigeria
options.c: VAT refunded by the NRS after an audit
options.d: VAT paid on purchases of raw inputs

questions.explanation: Output VAT is the VAT a business adds to its own sales. Option D describes input VAT, and B is import VAT, which for the importer is an input tax.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.155, the result of 'output VAT minus recoverable input VAT' measures:

options.a: The total VAT borne by the final consumer
options.b: The net VAT to remit to the NRS, or to claim as a refund or credit if negative
options.c: The VAT due on imported goods
options.d: The taxable person's profit for the month

questions.explanation: Output VAT less recoverable input VAT is the net position: a positive figure is paid to the NRS, and a negative figure becomes a refund or credit. Option A is wrong because the consumer's burden equals VAT on the final price, not one trader's net figure.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.185, which of the following is an EXEMPT supply?
questions.explanation: Baby products are on the exempt list in s.185. Basic food, exported services and fertilisers (options D, B, C) are zero-rated under s.186, so their suppliers can still recover input VAT.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.186, which of the following is ZERO-RATED?
questions.explanation: Medical and pharmaceutical products are zero-rated, so suppliers charge 0% and recover input VAT. Land and buildings, money and securities, and government licences (options D, C, A) are exempt under s.185.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a zero-rated supply under the NTA 2025, s.186?

options.d: Exported goods other than oil and gas

questions.explanation: Oil and gas exports are EXEMPT under s.185, so oil and gas exporters cannot recover input VAT on them. Exported services, educational books and non-oil exports (B, C, D) are zero-rated.

questions.question: Yaba Code Ltd, a Nigerian software company, sells its services only to clients in the United States. Under the NTA 2025, how are these supplies treated for VAT?

options.a: Outside VAT entirely, with no registration duty
options.b: Exempt: no output VAT, and input VAT is a cost
options.c: Zero-rated: no output VAT, and input VAT on its costs is recoverable
options.d: Taxable at 7.5%, because the supplier is in Nigeria

questions.explanation: The NTA expressly zero-rates exported services, so the firm charges 0% but reclaims VAT on its inputs, which keeps its prices competitive abroad. Option B treats the exports as exempt, which would make its input VAT an unrecoverable cost.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.22(1), by when must a taxable person file its monthly VAT return?

options.a: On or before the 30th day of the same month
options.b: Within 6 months of the end of the accounting year
options.c: On or before the 21st day of the month following the month of the transactions
options.d: On or before the 10th day of the following quarter

questions.explanation: Section 22(1) requires monthly VAT returns by the 21st day of the following month, whether or not there was activity. The other options describe deadlines that apply to no VAT return.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025 (with s.22 on VAT returns), a 'small business' (freed from the obligation to charge VAT and file VAT returns) is one with:

options.a: Total fixed assets below N100,000,000, including professional firms
options.b: Gross turnover of N25,000,000 or less a year, whatever its trade
options.c: Gross turnover of N100,000,000 or less a year and total fixed assets within N250,000,000, excluding providers of professional services
options.d: Fewer than 50 employees and turnover below N50,000,000

questions.explanation: The NTAA defines a small business by both a N100 million turnover limit and a N250 million fixed-asset limit, and professional service providers are excluded. Option B is the old N25 million administrative threshold.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, Okoye & Partners, a law firm with annual turnover of N60,000,000 and fixed assets of N20,000,000, claims it is a 'small business' that need not file VAT returns. Is the claim correct?

options.a: Yes, because its fixed assets are below N250,000,000
options.b: No, because providers of professional services are excluded from the small business definition
options.c: Yes, because its turnover is below N100,000,000
options.d: No, because only companies with turnover below N25,000,000 qualify

questions.explanation: Although the firm's figures are within both limits, professional service providers are expressly excluded from the small business definition, so it must charge VAT and file returns. Options C and A each look at one limit and ignore the exclusion.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.56, what are the time limits for a VAT refund?

options.a: Request within 30 days; NRS to refund within 12 months
options.b: Request within 12 months of the transaction; NRS to refund (or set off) within 30 days of a valid request
options.c: Request within 6 years; NRS to refund within 90 days
options.d: Request within 90 days; NRS to refund within 21 days

questions.explanation: Section 56 requires the claim within 12 months of the transaction and obliges the NRS to refund or set off within 30 days of receiving it. Option C mixes in the six-year claim period and 90-day refund period for general (non-VAT) refunds under s.55.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.81(2), on what basis is VAT revenue distributed among the States and among the Local Governments?

options.c: 50% by derivation, 30% by land mass, 20% equally
options.d: 100% according to where VAT returns are filed

questions.explanation: Section 81(2) shares the pool 50% equally, 20% on population and 30% on consumption. Option D is ruled out because consumption is measured by where goods and services are consumed, not where returns are filed.

questions.question: A Lagos-headquartered bank files all its VAT returns in Lagos, but most of the services on which it charged VAT were consumed by customers in Kano. Under the NTAA 2025, s.81, how is the consumption-based part of VAT distribution determined?

options.a: By the state where the company's head office is located
options.b: By the state where the VAT return is filed
options.c: By the population of the state where the company was incorporated
options.d: By the place of consumption, irrespective of where the return is filed

questions.explanation: The Act says consumption is determined by the place of consumption, irrespective of where the return is filed, so Kano benefits from consumption there. Options A and B describe the head-office bias that this rule was designed to remove.

questions.question: How does VAT under the NTA 2025 differ from the old single-stage Sales Tax that it replaced?

options.a: VAT covers goods only, while Sales Tax covered goods and services
options.b: VAT is charged only once at the retail stage, like Sales Tax
options.c: VAT is administered by each State, while Sales Tax was federal
options.d: VAT is charged at each stage with credit for input tax, removing the cascading 'tax-on-tax' effect

questions.explanation: VAT is multi-stage with an input credit, so tax is not charged on tax. The old Sales Tax had no credit mechanism, covered goods only and was State-administered, which is why options A and C reverse the facts.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.150, what is the VAT position of a non-resident company that supplies taxable services to persons in Nigeria?

options.a: It must register for VAT and charge Nigerian VAT on those supplies
options.b: It pays VAT only on goods, never on services
options.c: It is outside the VAT net because it has no Nigerian office
options.d: It may choose freely whether to charge VAT

questions.explanation: The NTA brings non-resident suppliers of taxable goods and services to Nigerian recipients into the VAT net, so they must register and charge VAT. Option C reflects the gap that the provision closes.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.149, VAT on imported goods is charged on:

options.c: The value of the goods including customs duty and other charges up to the point of entry
options.d: The importer's expected selling price in Nigeria

questions.explanation: The VAT base for imports is the customs (CIF) value plus duties and other charges, so VAT is effectively charged on duty as well. Option A leaves out insurance, freight and duty.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, which change was made to the recovery of input VAT compared with the old VAT Act?

options.a: Input VAT is now claimable only on goods bought for resale
options.b: Input VAT on services and fixed assets used for taxable supplies is now claimable
options.c: Input VAT can now be claimed on exempt supplies
options.d: Input VAT recovery was abolished for exporters

questions.explanation: The old law effectively limited input credit to goods for resale or direct use in production; the NTA allows recovery on services and fixed assets used for taxable supplies. Option A describes the old narrow rule, and C is wrong because exempt-related input VAT is still a cost.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.101, what is the administrative penalty for failing to file a return?

options.a: N50,000 for the first month and N25,000 for each subsequent month
options.c: N100,000 for the first month and N50,000 for each subsequent month
options.d: 10% per annum of the tax plus interest at the MPR

questions.explanation: Section 101 charges N100,000 in the first month and N50,000 for each later month the failure continues. Option A is the failure-to-register penalty under s.100, and D is the late-remittance penalty.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.100, what is the administrative penalty for failing to register as required?

options.b: N100,000 for the first month and N50,000 for each subsequent month
options.d: N50,000 for the first month and N25,000 for each subsequent month

questions.explanation: Section 100 imposes N50,000 for the first month and N25,000 for each subsequent month. Option B is the failure-to-file penalty, and N5,000,000 in A is the separate penalty on a body that awards a contract to an unregistered person.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, money and securities are exempt supplies under s.185. Ikeja Finance Ltd, whose only supplies are financial dealings in money and securities, buys office furniture and pays VAT on it. What happens to the VAT it paid on the furniture?

options.a: It is set off against the company's WHT
options.b: It is an irrecoverable cost to the company
options.c: It is passed on to the State government

questions.explanation: A supplier making only exempt supplies cannot recover input VAT, so the VAT becomes part of its costs. Option D would be right only if its supplies were zero-rated or taxable.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, VAT is charged on 'goods' and 'services'. For VAT purposes, 'goods' means:

options.b: Tangible and intangible property, including shares
options.d: All forms of tangible property, movable or immovable

questions.explanation: For VAT, goods cover all tangible property, movable or immovable, although supplies of land and buildings are then exempt. Option B is wrong because money and securities are not goods and are exempt anyway.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, a UK consultant advises a Lagos company by video call, and the advice is used in Lagos. Is this a taxable supply of a service in Nigeria?

options.a: No, because services received from abroad are exempt
options.b: Yes, because the service is provided to and consumed by a person in Nigeria
options.c: Yes, but only if the consultant visits Nigeria
options.d: No, because the consultant is physically outside Nigeria

questions.explanation: A service is treated as supplied in Nigeria where it is provided to and consumed by a person in Nigeria, wherever it is performed. Options D and C focus wrongly on where the supplier physically is.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, which of these is EXEMPT from VAT under s.185?

options.d: Goods and services purchased by diplomatic missions
