questions.explanation: Supplies to diplomatic missions are now on the exempt list. Educational books, medical services and exported services (options B, A, C) are zero-rated.

questions.question: Under the Ninth Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, what ad valorem stamp duty rate applies to a lease granted for a term of 12 years?
questions.explanation: A lease for a term of more than 7 years but not more than 21 years attracts 3% under the Ninth Schedule, so a 12-year lease falls in this band. Option B is the rate for short leases of up to 7 years. Option D is the figure wrongly applied to such leases in some older materials, and option C is the rate for a conveyance on sale.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, within what period after execution must a chargeable instrument be stamped?
questions.explanation: The 2025 Act requires a chargeable instrument to be stamped within 30 days of execution, harmonising the timeline. Option D was the period under the repealed Stamp Duties Act. Options C and A are not the statutory period.

questions.question: Under section 110 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, what is the penalty for failing to stamp a dutiable instrument on time?

options.a: Double the duty, with no interest
options.b: 40% of the unpaid duty with no interest
options.c: A flat N50,000 for each instrument
options.d: 10% of the unpaid duty plus interest at the prevailing CBN monetary policy rate

questions.explanation: Section 110 NTAA 2025 makes the person liable to pay 10% of the unpaid duty plus interest at the prevailing CBN monetary policy rate, in addition to the duty itself. Option B borrows the 40% figure from the penalty for failure to deduct withholding tax. Options C and A are not the statutory penalty.

questions.question: What is the main legal consequence of leaving a dutiable instrument, such as a company's lease, unstamped under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025?

options.a: The lease becomes void and the tenant must vacate
options.b: The instrument is valid only if registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission
options.c: It cannot be used even in criminal proceedings
options.d: It cannot be admitted in evidence in civil court or arbitration proceedings until it is properly stamped

questions.explanation: An unstamped instrument is not void, but it cannot be relied on as evidence in civil or arbitral proceedings, which leaves the parties unable to enforce it until it is stamped. Option A overstates the effect, because the agreement still exists. Option C is wrong because unstamped instruments may still be admitted in criminal proceedings.

questions.question: Under the Ninth Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, in 2026: a company buys land and buildings for a consideration of N250,000,000. Conveyance on sale is charged at 1.5% ad valorem. What stamp duty is payable, and by whom?
questions.explanation: Duty on a conveyance on sale is N250,000,000 x 1.5% = N3,750,000, and it is borne by the transferee, the buyer who needs a properly stamped title document. Option B has the right amount but the wrong party. Option D uses the 0.78% short-lease rate, and option C uses 3%.

questions.question: Under the Ninth Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, in 2026: a company takes a 20-year lease at an annual rent of N12,000,000. Duty on a lease of more than 7 but not more than 21 years is charged at 3% of the annual rent. What stamp duty is payable?
questions.explanation: A 20-year lease falls in the more-than-7-years band, so duty is N12,000,000 x 3% = N360,000. Option B uses the 0.78% rate for leases of up to 7 years. Option D uses 6%, and option A wrongly applies 3% to the total rent for all 20 years.

questions.question: Under the Ninth Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, in 2026: a new company registers with nominal (authorised) share capital of N5,000,000. Capital duty is 0.75% of the share capital. How much capital duty is payable?
questions.explanation: Capital duty is N5,000,000 x 0.75% = N37,500, paid by the company on its authorised share capital. Option D uses 1.5%, option C uses 0.125%, and option B misplaces the decimal (0.075%).

questions.question: Under the Ninth Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, in 2026: a bank processes 300,000 electronic transfers of N10,000 or more (none of them salary payments or transfers between a customer's own accounts in the same bank). Each attracts a fixed stamp duty of N50. What total duty is due?

options.d: Nil, because electronic transfers are exempt

questions.explanation: Every qualifying electronic transfer of N10,000 or more attracts N50, so 300,000 x N50 = N15,000,000. Options A and C misplace a zero. Option D is wrong because only transfers below N10,000, salary payments and intra-bank self-transfers are exempt.

questions.question: Under the Ninth Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, in 2026: stamp duty of N360,000 on a company's lease is paid 3 months late. Under section 110 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 the penalty is 10% of the unpaid duty plus interest at the CBN monetary policy rate. Ignoring interest, what is the total of duty plus penalty?
questions.explanation: The penalty is 10% x N360,000 = N36,000, so the duty plus penalty is N396,000, with interest at the CBN monetary policy rate added on top. Option D ignores the penalty. Option A wrongly charges 10% for each month late, and option C applies a 40% penalty, which belongs to failure to deduct withholding tax.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 (NTA), Ninth Schedule, a conveyance or transfer on sale of real property attracts ad valorem stamp duty at 1.5% of the consideration, payable by the transferee. Ajah Holdings Ltd buys an office building for N80,000,000. What stamp duty is payable?
questions.explanation: Stamp duty = N80,000,000 x 1.5% = N1,200,000, paid by Ajah Holdings as transferee. Option B misplaces the decimal (15%), and A uses the 0.75% share capital rate.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, a lease of not more than 7 years attracts stamp duty at 0.78% of the annual rent, payable by the lessee. Gbagada Clinic Ltd signs a 5-year lease at an annual rent of N6,000,000. What stamp duty is payable?
questions.explanation: Stamp duty = annual rent x 0.78% = N6,000,000 x 0.78% = N46,800. Option B applies the rate to the total rent for 5 years instead of to the annual rent, and A uses the rate for leases above 7 years.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, a lease of more than 7 years (and not more than 21 years) attracts stamp duty at 3% of the annual rent. Oregun Tech Ltd signs a 15-year office lease at an annual rent of N10,000,000. What stamp duty is payable?
questions.explanation: Stamp duty = N10,000,000 x 3% = N300,000, based on one year's rent. Option B uses the 0.78% rate for short leases, D uses 6%, a figure from old practice, and C applies 3% to all 15 years of rent.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, capital duty on share capital is 0.75% of the nominal share capital. Lekki Ventures Ltd is incorporated with nominal share capital of N20,000,000. What capital duty is payable?
questions.explanation: Capital duty = N20,000,000 x 0.75% = N150,000. Option B misplaces the decimal (7.5%), and A uses the 0.125% loan capital rate.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, duty on share capital is 0.75% and, when share capital is increased, it is charged on the amount of the increase. Ilupeju Foods Ltd increases its share capital from N10,000,000 to N25,000,000. What duty is payable on the increase?
questions.explanation: Duty = (N25,000,000 - N10,000,000) x 0.75% = N15,000,000 x 0.75% = N112,500. Option A charges the full new share capital, which would tax the N10,000,000 a second time.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, duty on loan capital is 0.125% of the amount secured. Kaduna Textiles Plc raises loan capital (debenture stock) of N120,000,000. What stamp duty is payable?
questions.explanation: Duty = N120,000,000 x 0.125% = N150,000. Option D misplaces the decimal (1.25%), and B uses the 0.75% share capital rate.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, a fixed stamp duty of N50 applies to each electronic receipt or transfer of N10,000 or more; under s.184, transfers below N10,000 and salary payments are exempt. In a month, Unity Bank processed 400,000 transfers of N10,000 or more, 150,000 transfers below N10,000, and 50,000 salary payments. What total duty should it collect?
questions.explanation: Only the 400,000 qualifying transfers bear duty: 400,000 x N50 = N20,000,000. Option D charges every transfer, C wrongly includes salary payments, and A wrongly includes transfers below N10,000.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, a N50 stamp duty applies to each electronic transfer of N10,000 or more, while transfers below N10,000 and transfers between a customer's own accounts in the same bank are exempt (s.184). In one day Amaka sends N9,500 to a friend, N10,000 to a tailor, N250,000 to a landlord, and moves N50,000 between her own two accounts in the same bank. How much stamp duty does she bear?
questions.explanation: Only the N10,000 and N250,000 transfers qualify (N10,000 meets the 'N10,000 or more' threshold): 2 x N50 = N100. Option C wrongly charges the self-transfer, B charges all four, and A treats N10,000 as below the threshold.

questions.question: Under the NTAA 2025, s.110, failure to stamp a dutiable instrument attracts a penalty of 10% of the unpaid duty plus interest at the CBN MPR. Duty of N360,000 was paid 90 days late when the MPR was 27%. Treat the 10% as a one-off charge and compute interest as simple interest on a days/365 basis. What is the total of penalty and interest, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Penalty = 10% x N360,000 = N36,000; interest = N360,000 x 27% x 90/365 = N23,967; total = N59,967. Option C forgets the interest, B forgets the penalty, and D charges a full year of interest.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, a lease of more than 7 years (not more than 21 years) attracts duty of 3% of annual rent, and under the NTAA 2025, s.110, late stamping adds a penalty of 10% of the unpaid duty plus MPR interest. Surulere Stores Ltd stamped a 10-year lease at annual rent of N9,000,000 after the deadline. Ignoring interest, what is the total of duty and penalty?
questions.explanation: Duty = N9,000,000 x 3% = N270,000; penalty = 10% x N270,000 = N27,000; total = N297,000. Option C applies the 10% penalty to the rent instead of the duty, and D uses the short-lease rate.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, agreements or contracts not otherwise specified attract a fixed duty of N1,000 each. Ikeja Facility Services Ltd signs 25 separate cleaning service agreements in a month. What total stamp duty is payable?
questions.explanation: Fixed duty = 25 x N1,000 = N25,000; a fixed duty does not depend on the contract value. Option C charges only one agreement, and A misplaces a zero.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.132, the transfer of a mineral asset (such as a mining lease) is dutiable at an ad valorem rate of 2% of the value of the transfer. Jos Tin Ltd acquires a mining lease for N300,000,000. What duty is payable?
questions.explanation: Duty = N300,000,000 x 2% = N6,000,000. Option C uses the 1.5% rate for conveyance of real property, which the NTA does not apply to mineral assets.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, conveyance on sale of real property attracts 1.5% of the consideration and a lease of not more than 7 years attracts 0.78% of the annual rent. In one month Agege Pharma Ltd buys a warehouse for N150,000,000 and signs a 3-year lease of a shop at an annual rent of N4,000,000. What total stamp duty does it pay?
questions.explanation: Conveyance duty = N150,000,000 x 1.5% = N2,250,000; lease duty = N4,000,000 x 0.78% = N31,200; total = N2,281,200. Option D applies the lease rate to three years' rent, and A charges 1.5% on the rent as well.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.125, a chargeable instrument must be stamped not later than 30 days after its execution. Ojota Motors Ltd executed a lease on 5 March 2026. What is the last day for stamping it?
questions.explanation: Thirty days after 5 March 2026 is 4 April 2026. Option B reflects the old 40-day period under the repealed Stamp Duties Act, and A confuses stamping with the 21st-day remittance date for deducted taxes.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, each electronic receipt or transfer of N10,000 or more attracts N50 stamp duty. A bank processed 50,000 transfers of N20,000 each from Apex Ltd's account. What total duty is due?
questions.explanation: The duty is a fixed N50 per qualifying transfer, whatever the amount: 50,000 x N50 = N2,500,000. Options A and D wrongly treat it as a percentage of the amount transferred.

questions.question: Following the 2025 tax reform, where are the main provisions on stamp duties now found (Nigeria Tax Act 2025 vs older law)?

options.a: Chapter Five of the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 (ss.123-142), with rates in the Ninth Schedule
options.c: Chapter Six of the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, with rates in the First Schedule
options.d: The Stamp Duties Act Cap. S8, LFN 2004, as amended

questions.explanation: The NTA repealed the Stamp Duties Act and moved stamp duties into Chapter Five, with the rates set out in the Ninth Schedule. Option D is the repealed law, and Chapter Six in C deals with VAT.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Chapter Five, a tax charged on written instruments (documents) such as conveyances, leases and agreements, rather than directly on income or consumption, is known as:
questions.explanation: Stamp duty is charged on instruments, and payment is shown by stamping or electronic tagging of the document. VAT (D) is a tax on consumption, and WHT (B) is an advance income tax.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.125, within what period must a chargeable instrument be stamped?

options.a: By the 21st day of the following month
options.d: Not later than 30 days after its execution

questions.explanation: Section 125 requires stamping within 30 days after execution. Option C was the period under the repealed Stamp Duties Act, and A is the remittance date for deducted taxes.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.126, what is the main consequence in civil proceedings of an instrument that has not been duly stamped?

options.a: It becomes void and unenforceable for all purposes
options.b: It is not admissible in evidence
options.c: It is automatically stamped by the court at double duty
options.d: It is admissible only if the parties agree

questions.explanation: An unstamped instrument cannot be admitted in evidence in civil proceedings until it is stamped, which is a strong incentive to comply. Option A goes too far: the document is not void, and it can be stamped later (with penalties) and then relied on.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.126, in which type of proceedings may an unstamped instrument still be admitted in evidence?

options.c: Civil proceedings in the High Court
options.d: Tax Appeal Tribunal proceedings on stamp duty

questions.explanation: The bar on unstamped instruments applies to civil and similar proceedings, but such an instrument may be admitted in criminal proceedings. Options C, B and D are all proceedings where the bar applies.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.124, which of the following is a recognised way of denoting that stamp duty has been paid?

options.d: Registration of the document at the CAC

questions.explanation: Section 124 recognises modern methods such as electronic or digital tagging and electronic receipts, alongside adhesive stamps and dies. The other options are not ways of denoting duty.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, an 'ad valorem' stamp duty is one that is:

options.a: Charged only on instruments executed abroad
options.b: Calculated as a percentage of the value or consideration in the instrument
options.c: Payable only by the State government
options.d: A fixed amount regardless of the value involved

questions.explanation: Ad valorem means 'according to value', so the duty rises with the consideration, as with 1.5% on a conveyance. Option D describes a fixed duty, such as N1,000 on an unspecified agreement.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, Ninth Schedule, which of these attracts a FIXED (not ad valorem) stamp duty?

options.a: Loan capital raised by a company
options.c: An agreement or contract not otherwise specified
options.d: A conveyance on sale of land

questions.explanation: Agreements or contracts not expressly specified carry a fixed N1,000 duty, whatever their value. Conveyances, leases and loan capital (options D, B, A) are charged as a percentage of value or rent.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, who is generally liable to pay stamp duty on a lease?
questions.explanation: The NTA follows the principle that the party who benefits pays, so the lessee (tenant) pays duty on a lease, just as the buyer pays on a conveyance. Option A is the landlord, who is not the liable party.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, who pays the stamp duty on a conveyance on sale of a building?

options.d: The lawyer who prepares the deed

questions.explanation: The NTA puts the duty on the person who benefits, which in a sale is the buyer (transferee). Option C is the seller, who receives the price and does not bear the duty.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.201, 'conveyance on sale' is limited to transfers of:

options.c: Any property, including shares and intellectual property

questions.explanation: The NTA defines conveyance on sale as the transfer of real property, so transfers of intangibles and other business assets no longer attract conveyance duty. Option C reflects the wider position under the repealed Act.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, from 1 January 2026, who bears the N50 stamp duty on an electronic transfer of N10,000 or more?

options.d: The bank, from its own funds

questions.explanation: The N50 duty, which replaced the Electronic Money Transfer Levy, is now deducted from the sender's account. Option C was the earlier practice under the EMTL, when the receiving account was charged.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.184, which of the following electronic transactions is NOT exempt from the N50 stamp duty?

options.a: A N15,000 transfer to a supplier at another bank
options.d: A transfer between two accounts of the same customer in the same bank

questions.explanation: A N15,000 transfer to a third party meets the N10,000 threshold and has no exemption, so N50 applies. Transfers below N10,000, salary payments and intra-bank self-transfers (options B, C, D) are all exempt.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.184, which of the following is exempt from stamp duty?

options.b: A conveyance of a factory to a company
options.c: Documents relating to the transfer of stocks and shares

questions.explanation: The exemption for documents relating to the transfer of stocks and shares carried over from the old Act into s.184. The conveyance, lease and mineral asset transfer (options B, D, A) are all dutiable.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.184, which of these instruments is exempt from stamp duty?

options.a: Instruments relating to the transfer of Government stocks or funds
options.c: A conveyance of land to a bank
options.d: A loan agreement between two companies

questions.explanation: Transfers of Government or legislative stocks or funds are listed exemptions. The other instruments (D, B, C) are ordinary dutiable instruments.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025 and NTAA 2025 division of stamp duty jurisdiction, which instrument falls under the State Internal Revenue Service rather than the Nigeria Revenue Service?

options.a: Memorandum and Articles of a new company
options.b: A tenancy agreement between two private individuals
options.c: A debenture issued by a company
options.d: Electronic transfer duty collected by banks

questions.explanation: Stamp duties on instruments executed by individuals, such as private tenancies, are State matters, while instruments executed by companies go to the NRS. Options C, A and D are all federal.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.142, Ikoyi Ltd transfers a building to Lekki Ltd in exchange for 10,000 cars instead of cash. How is the stamp duty value determined?

options.a: By the original cost of the building to Ikoyi Ltd
options.b: By reference to the fair market value of the non-monetary consideration
options.c: Nil duty, because no money changed hands
options.d: At a fixed duty of N1,000

questions.explanation: The NTA has a specific provision for non-monetary consideration such as barter, valuing it at fair market value. Option C reflects the loophole the provision closes.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, a property sale is documented in a sale agreement, a deed of assignment and a receipt, all for the same transaction. How is stamp duty applied?

options.b: None is dutiable because they duplicate each other
options.c: Only one instrument bears ad valorem duty; the others are stamped at a fixed duty
options.d: All three instruments bear full ad valorem duty

questions.explanation: Where several instruments cover the same transaction, the NTA charges ad valorem duty on one and a fixed duty on the others, which avoids taxing one deal several times. Option D is the double charge the rule avoids.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, which rate structure applies to leases in the Ninth Schedule for a lease of not more than 7 years?

options.d: 1.5% of the total rent for the term

questions.explanation: Short leases of up to 7 years attract 0.78% of the annual rent. Option C is the rate for longer leases, and D confuses the lease rate with the conveyance rate.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, which tax authority has jurisdiction over stamp duties on instruments executed by companies?
questions.explanation: Stamp duties on instruments executed by companies are federal and collected by the NRS. State IRSs (C) handle instruments executed by individuals, and the CAC (A) registers companies but does not collect stamp duty.

questions.question: What happened to the Electronic Money Transfer Levy (EMTL) under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025?

options.a: It was moved into withholding tax at 2%
options.b: It was abolished with no replacement
options.c: It was converted into a 0.5% VAT on all transfers
options.d: It was replaced by a N50 stamp duty on electronic transfers of N10,000 or more under the NTA 2025

questions.explanation: The EMTL introduced by the Finance Acts was replaced by a N50 stamp duty in the NTA's Ninth Schedule on electronic receipts or transfers of N10,000 or more. The other options describe changes that did not happen.

questions.question: Under the NTA 2025, s.132, how is the transfer of a mineral asset (such as a mining licence or lease) treated for stamp duty?

options.a: It is dutiable at 2% of the value of the transfer
options.b: It is exempt as a government licence
options.c: It is charged at the 1.5% conveyance rate
options.d: It attracts only a fixed N1,000 duty

questions.explanation: The NTA has a specific provision on mineral assets, charging 2% ad valorem on the transfer value. Option C is wrong because conveyance duty now applies only to real property.

questions.question: Which law did the NTA 2025 repeal in consolidating stamp duties into Chapter Five?

options.a: The Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020
options.d: The Stamp Duties Act, Cap. S8, LFN 2004

questions.explanation: The NTA repealed the Stamp Duties Act (as amended by the Finance Acts) and moved its substance into Chapter Five and the Ninth Schedule. The other laws were not repealed by the NTA.

questions.question: Cresta Beverages Ltd imports spirits from Scotland in 2026 with a CIF value of $800,000. The exchange rate is $1 = N1,700. The ECOWAS Common External Tariff rate on the spirits is 35% of the CIF value. What is the import duty payable?
questions.explanation: Customs value is CIF converted to naira: $800,000 x N1,700 = N1,360,000,000, and duty at 35% is N476,000,000. Option B forgets to convert to naira. Option C uses a 10% band, and option D is the duty-paid value (CIF plus duty), not the duty.

questions.question: Cresta Beverages Ltd imports spirits from Scotland in 2026 with a CIF value of $800,000. The exchange rate is $1 = N1,700. Import duty is 35% of CIF. Taking the VAT base on importation as CIF plus import duty, and VAT at 7.5% under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, what VAT is payable on importation?
questions.explanation: CIF is N1,360,000,000 and duty is N476,000,000, so the VAT base is N1,836,000,000 and VAT at 7.5% is N137,700,000. Option C charges VAT on CIF alone, leaving out the duty. Option A charges VAT on the duty only, and option D uses 10%.

questions.question: Cresta Beverages Ltd imports spirits from Scotland in 2026 with a CIF value of $800,000. The exchange rate is $1 = N1,700. The ECOWAS Trade Levy is 0.5% of the CIF value. What is the levy?
questions.explanation: The levy is N1,360,000,000 x 0.5% = N6,800,000. Option C uses 5% and option D uses 1%. Option B wrongly applies 0.5% to the import duty instead of the CIF value.

questions.question: Cresta Beverages Ltd exports beer made partly from imported inputs on which it paid import duty. Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023, what is manufacturing drawback?

options.a: A refund of the import duty paid on imported inputs used in making goods that are later exported
options.b: A VAT credit given only to exporters
options.c: A refund of company income tax on export profits
options.d: An extra excise duty charged on exported beer

questions.explanation: Manufacturing drawback refunds import duty on imported inputs in proportion to their content in goods that are exported, so exporters are not burdened with duty on materials that leave the country inside their products. Option D is the opposite of a relief. Options B and C confuse drawback with VAT and income tax rules.

questions.question: Which statement best describes excise duty as it applies to beer brewed locally by Cresta Beverages Ltd?

options.a: A tax on the brewery's annual profits
options.b: A tax charged only when the beer is exported
options.c: A duty on imported goods, charged on their CIF value at the port
options.d: A duty on goods manufactured in Nigeria, charged on production at the factory, often as a specific amount per litre plus an ad valorem percentage

questions.explanation: Excise duty is a tax on selected locally manufactured goods such as beer, spirits and tobacco, charged at the factory gate, typically as a specific rate per unit plus a percentage of value. Option C describes customs import duty. Option A describes company income tax, and option B is wrong because exports are generally relieved rather than targeted.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023, import duty in Nigeria is computed on the customs value of goods, which in practice is the CIF value. What does CIF stand for?
questions.explanation: CIF means Cost, Insurance and Freight: the price of the goods plus the insurance and freight needed to bring them to the Nigerian port. Option A replaces insurance with inspection and fees, which are separate charges, while Option B wrongly puts customs into the value on which customs duty is itself charged.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 framework, on which value is import duty normally computed for goods imported into Nigeria?

options.a: The expected retail selling price in Nigeria
options.b: The ex-factory price of the goods in Nigeria
options.c: The CIF value of the goods, converted to naira
options.d: The FOB value of the goods only

questions.explanation: Import duty is charged on the CIF value, that is the cost of the goods plus insurance and freight to Nigeria, converted to naira. Option D leaves out insurance and freight, and Option B is the base for excise duty on locally manufactured goods, not for import duty.

questions.question: Nigeria applies the ECOWAS Common External Tariff (CET) to classify import duty rates. Which set correctly lists the five CET duty bands?
questions.explanation: The ECOWAS CET has five bands: 0%, 5%, 10%, 20% and 35%, rising from essential inputs to finished goods the region wants to protect. Option C invents a 15% and 25% band, and Option A confuses the VAT rate of 7.5% with a tariff band.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five ECOWAS Common External Tariff bands applied to imports into Nigeria?
questions.explanation: The five CET bands are 0%, 5%, 10%, 20% and 35%, so 15% is not a band. Options A, C and D are all genuine CET rates, with 35% being the highest band.

questions.question: An importer in Apapa is told that the highest ECOWAS Common External Tariff band applies to his consignment. What import duty rate is that?
questions.explanation: The top CET band is 35%, and like every band it is applied to the CIF value. Option A is the next band down, and Option D uses the wrong base because duty is not charged on FOB value alone.

questions.question: A duty charged on goods manufactured within Nigeria, imposed at the ex-factory stage on items such as beer, spirits, tobacco and sugar-sweetened beverages, is called:
questions.explanation: Excise duty is levied on locally manufactured goods at the ex-factory gate. Option A applies to goods brought into Nigeria from abroad, Option C is a general consumption tax on most supplies, and Option D is a refund of duty, not a charge.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes excise duty in Nigeria?

options.a: A duty on all goods entering Nigeria, charged on CIF value
options.b: A refund of duty paid on imported inputs used for exports
options.c: A duty on selected goods manufactured in Nigeria, charged on quantity and/or ex-factory value
options.d: A tax on every supply of goods and services, charged at 7.5%

questions.explanation: Excise duty targets selected locally manufactured goods and is charged per unit, as a percentage of the ex-factory price, or both. Option A describes import duty, Option D describes VAT and Option B describes duty drawback.

questions.question: What is the main difference between import duty and excise duty in Nigeria?

options.a: Import duty is charged on goods brought into Nigeria; excise duty is charged on goods manufactured in Nigeria
options.b: Import duty is charged on services; excise duty is charged on goods
options.c: Import duty is charged at 7.5%; excise duty is charged at 35%
options.d: Import duty is charged on exports; excise duty is charged on imports

questions.explanation: The two duties are separated by where the goods come from: import duty falls on imports at CIF value, while excise duty falls on local production at the ex-factory stage. Option B is wrong because no customs duty is charged on services, and Option C confuses the VAT rate and the top CET band with the duties themselves.

questions.question: In excise duty, what is a 'specific' rate?

options.a: A rate fixed separately for each manufacturer by negotiation
options.b: A percentage of the CIF value of imported goods
options.c: A fixed amount charged per unit of quantity, such as per litre or per stick
options.d: A percentage of the ex-factory value of the goods

questions.explanation: A specific rate is a fixed naira amount per unit, for example per litre of beer or per stick of cigarettes, regardless of price. Option D describes an ad valorem rate, and Option B describes how import duty is charged.

questions.question: An excise rate expressed as a percentage of the ex-factory price of the goods is known as:
questions.explanation: Ad valorem means 'according to value', so the duty rises with the ex-factory price. Options B and C both describe a fixed amount per litre or per stick, which does not change with price.

questions.question: Excise on beer is charged as a fixed amount per litre plus a percentage of the ex-factory price. Such a duty is best described as:

options.a: A compound duty, combining a specific and an ad valorem element
options.b: A customs duty charged on the CIF value
options.c: A purely ad valorem duty charged on value only
options.d: A purely specific duty charged per litre only

questions.explanation: When a per-unit amount and a percentage of value are both charged on the same product, the duty is compound (mixed). Options C and D each capture only one of the two elements, and Option B applies to imports, not local brewing.

questions.question: Which of the following products is most typically subject to excise duty in Nigeria?

options.a: Legal services supplied by a law firm
options.b: Sugar-sweetened beverages produced by a local bottler
options.d: Unprocessed yams sold by a farmer

questions.explanation: Sugar-sweetened beverages appear in the Nigerian excise schedule alongside beer, spirits, wine and tobacco. Option D is unprocessed farm produce, Option A is a service, and Option C is an import that bears customs charges rather than excise on local manufacture.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an excisable product in the Nigerian excise schedule?

options.c: Fresh tomatoes sold in a local market
options.d: Spirits such as gin and vodka

questions.explanation: Excise in Nigeria targets manufactured products such as beer, spirits, wine, tobacco and sugar-sweetened beverages, not fresh farm produce. Options A, B and D are all listed excisable products.

questions.question: What is 'duty drawback' under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 framework?

options.a: A penalty for importing goods without a pre-arrival declaration
options.b: A discount on excise for manufacturers who produce above a set volume
options.c: An additional duty charged on luxury imports
options.d: A refund of import duty paid on goods that are re-exported or used to make goods that are exported

questions.explanation: Duty drawback gives back import duty when the imported goods, or the inputs inside exported products, leave Nigeria, so exports are not burdened with Nigerian import duty. Option C describes a surcharge, which increases duty rather than refunding it.

questions.question: Kano Traders Ltd imported a consignment, paid import duty, and later re-exported the entire consignment unused. Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 drawback rules, how much of the import duty can be reclaimed?

options.a: None, because duty is never refundable
options.c: Only the VAT paid on importation

questions.explanation: Goods imported and re-exported unused qualify for a 100% drawback of the duty paid on them. Option B has no basis in the drawback rules, and Option A ignores the drawback scheme altogether.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 framework, a 'manufacturing drawback' refunds:

options.a: VAT charged on locally purchased raw materials
options.b: Excise duty paid on goods sold in Nigeria
options.c: All import duty paid by a manufacturer in the year, whether or not it exports
options.d: Import duty on imported inputs in proportion to their content in manufactured goods that are exported

questions.explanation: Manufacturing drawback is proportionate: only the duty on the imported inputs that end up in exported products is refunded. Option C ignores the export link, and Options A and B concern excise and VAT rather than import duty.

questions.question: Which law is the primary legislation for the administration and computation of customs (import) duty in Nigeria after the 2025 tax reforms?
questions.explanation: Customs duty was not absorbed into the Nigeria Tax Act 2025; it remains governed by the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 with ECOWAS CET rates. Option A consolidated income tax, VAT and stamp duties but not customs duty, and Option B has been repealed.

questions.question: The Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 repealed which earlier law that had governed customs and excise administration in Nigeria?

options.a: The Customs and Excise Management Act (CEMA)

questions.explanation: The Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 replaced the Customs and Excise Management Act (CEMA), Cap. C45, as the main customs statute. Options B, C and D were repealed by the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, not by the customs law.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about customs duty after the 2025 tax reforms is NOT correct?

options.a: Import duty rates follow the ECOWAS Common External Tariff
options.b: Customs duty remains governed by the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023
options.c: Customs duty was absorbed into the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and is now charged under it
options.d: Import duty is charged on the CIF value of imported goods

questions.explanation: The 2025 reforms consolidated income tax, VAT and stamp duties into the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, but customs duty stayed under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023. Options A, B and D are all correct statements, so they are not the answer.

questions.question: Lagos Design Studio Ltd pays a firm in London for architectural drawings delivered by email. Which of the following can NEVER be charged on this import of a service?

options.d: Stamp duty on a written contract for the work

questions.explanation: Customs duty is charged on goods at their CIF value, so there is no customs duty on an imported service. VAT, withholding tax and stamp duty in Options A, C and D may still need to be considered under their own rules, so they cannot be ruled out in the same way.

questions.question: Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023, what is the primary method of valuing imported goods for customs purposes?

options.a: A value fixed by the importer in a sworn declaration, without reference to the price
options.b: Transaction value: the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to Nigeria
options.c: The value of identical goods imported in the last five years
options.d: The retail price of similar goods in Lagos markets

questions.explanation: Customs valuation starts with the transaction value, the price actually paid or payable, following the WTO approach; other methods are fall-backs. Option C is a secondary method used only when transaction value cannot be used, and Option D would tax the importer's later mark-up.

questions.question: An importer buys goods from its parent company abroad, and the relationship has clearly influenced the invoice price. Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023, which valuation approach should Customs move to?

options.a: A value equal to the importer's expected selling price minus VAT
options.b: The invoice price, because transaction value always applies
options.c: The FOB value with no adjustment
options.d: The value of identical or similar goods imported at about the same time

questions.explanation: Transaction value cannot be used where the buyer and seller are related and the relationship has influenced the price, so Customs falls back on the value of identical or similar goods. Option B ignores that exception, and Option C still relies on the influenced price.

questions.question: Why is VAT on an imported item normally higher than 7.5% of its CIF value?

options.a: Because the VAT base on importation includes the import duty as well as the CIF value
options.b: Because VAT on imports is charged at 10% instead of 7.5%
options.c: Because VAT on imports is charged on the retail price
options.d: Because VAT on imports is charged on the FOB value plus a 20% mark-up

questions.explanation: VAT on imported goods is computed on the CIF value plus import duty, so it is VAT charged partly on the duty. Option B is wrong because the rate is still 7.5%, and Options C and D invent bases that the framework does not use.

questions.question: The rationale usually given for excise duty on products such as sugar-sweetened beverages and tobacco is that it:

options.a: Protects local manufacturers from competing imported products
options.b: Refunds import duty to exporters of manufactured goods
options.c: Raises revenue while discouraging consumption of goods considered harmful
options.d: Replaces VAT on those products so they are not taxed twice

questions.explanation: Excise is often called a 'sin tax': it raises revenue and, by raising the price, discourages consumption of harmful products. Option A is the protective role of import tariffs, and Option D is wrong because VAT still applies alongside excise.

questions.question: For a locally manufactured excisable product, the ad valorem element of excise duty is calculated on:

options.a: The CIF value of the goods
options.b: The ex-factory price of the goods
options.c: The cost of imported raw materials only

questions.explanation: The ad valorem part of excise is a percentage of the ex-factory price, the value at the factory gate. Option A is the import duty base, and Option D would charge excise on distributor margins and VAT.

questions.question: Owerri Medicals Ltd imported equipment with FOB value $50,000, insurance $1,000 and freight $4,000. The exchange rate is $1 = N1,500. Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023, what is the CIF value in naira?
questions.explanation: CIF = (FOB + insurance + freight) x exchange rate = ($50,000 + $1,000 + $4,000) x 1,500 = N82,500,000. Option B uses FOB only, and Option D forgets insurance.

questions.question: Goods with FOB value $50,000, insurance $1,000 and freight $4,000 are imported at $1 = N1,500. The ECOWAS CET rate is 10%. Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023, what is the import duty?
questions.explanation: Import duty = CET rate x CIF = 10% x N82,500,000 = N8,250,000. Option C applies 10% to FOB only, and Option D wrongly applies the VAT rate instead of the CET rate.

questions.question: Ikeja Electronics Ltd imported goods with a CIF value of N40,000,000. Import duty is 20% of CIF. VAT at 7.5% is charged on CIF plus import duty (no other charges are in the VAT base). What is the VAT on importation?
questions.explanation: VAT base = CIF + duty = N40,000,000 + N8,000,000 = N48,000,000; VAT = 7.5% x N48,000,000 = N3,600,000. Option B forgets to add the duty to the base, and Option C charges VAT on the duty alone.

questions.question: Benin Diagnostics Ltd imported laboratory equipment: FOB EUR80,000, insurance EUR1,500, freight EUR3,500; EUR1 = N1,800. Assume: import duty 5% of CIF; CISS levy 1% of CIF; ECOWAS levy 0.5% of CIF; VAT 7.5% on (CIF + import duty). What are the total import charges, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: CIF = EUR85,000 x 1,800 = N153,000,000. Duty N7,650,000 + CISS N1,530,000 + ECOWAS N765,000 + VAT 7.5% x N160,650,000 = N12,048,750; total N21,993,750. Option D leaves out VAT, and Option B computes VAT on CIF only.

questions.question: Aba Foods Ltd imported packaged food with a CIF value of $25,000 at $1 = N1,600. Assume: import duty 20% of CIF; CISS levy 1% of CIF; ECOWAS levy 0.5% of CIF; NAFDAC levy 0.5% of CIF; VAT 7.5% on (CIF + import duty). What are the total import charges?
questions.explanation: CIF = 25,000 x 1,600 = N40,000,000. Duty N8,000,000 + CISS N400,000 + ECOWAS N200,000 + NAFDAC N200,000 + VAT 7.5% x N48,000,000 = N3,600,000; total N12,400,000. Option B forgets the NAFDAC levy, which applies to food, drugs and cosmetics, and Option D leaves the duty out of the VAT base.

questions.question: An importer paid import duty of N4,200,000 on goods with a CIF value of N12,000,000. Under the ECOWAS Common External Tariff, which band was applied?
questions.explanation: CET rate = duty / CIF = N4,200,000 / N12,000,000 = 35%, the top CET band. Option B divides by the wrong figure, and Option C is the next band down.

questions.question: Goods with a CIF value of N30,000,000 attract import duty at 10% under the ECOWAS CET. Assume a surcharge of 7% of the import duty also applies. What is the total of import duty plus surcharge?
questions.explanation: Duty = 10% x N30,000,000 = N3,000,000; surcharge = 7% x N3,000,000 = N210,000; total N3,210,000. Option D wrongly computes the surcharge on CIF instead of on the duty, and Option B forgets the surcharge.

questions.question: Machinery is bought for FOB $60,000 with freight of $6,000. Insurance is 1% of (FOB + freight). The exchange rate is $1 = N1,550. What is the CIF value in naira for customs purposes, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Insurance = 1% x $66,000 = $660; CIF = $66,660 x 1,550 = N103,323,000. Option C ignores insurance, and Option A calculates insurance on FOB only.

questions.question: Enugu Breweries Ltd produced 200,000 litres of beer at an ex-factory price of N500 per litre. Assume excise on beer is N0.30 per litre plus 20% ad valorem on the ex-factory value. What is the total excise duty?
questions.explanation: Specific: 200,000 x N0.30 = N60,000; ad valorem: 200,000 x N500 x 20% = N20,000,000; total N20,060,000. Option A forgets the specific element, and Option B forgets the ad valorem element.

questions.question: A distillery in Ota produced 50,000 litres of gin at an ex-factory price of N2,000 per litre. Assume excise on spirits is N1.50 per litre plus 30% ad valorem. What is the excise duty payable?
questions.explanation: Specific: 50,000 x N1.50 = N75,000; ad valorem: 50,000 x N2,000 x 30% = N30,000,000; total N30,075,000. Option A leaves out the per-litre charge, and Option C uses the beer ad valorem rate of 20% instead of 30%.

questions.question: A tobacco manufacturer produced 2,000,000 cigarette sticks with an ex-factory price of N40 per stick. Assume excise on cigarettes is N3.50 per stick plus 20% ad valorem. What is the excise duty?
questions.explanation: Specific: 2,000,000 x N3.50 = N7,000,000; ad valorem: 2,000,000 x N40 x 20% = N16,000,000; total N23,000,000. Option A ignores the ad valorem part, and Option D wrongly applies 20% to the specific duty plus price.

questions.question: A juice bottler produced 80,000 litres of a sugar-sweetened beverage. Assume excise is N0.10 per centilitre (1 litre = 100 centilitres). What is the excise duty?
questions.explanation: Volume in centilitres = 80,000 x 100 = 8,000,000 cl; excise = 8,000,000 x N0.10 = N800,000. Option A applies the rate per litre, forgetting to convert to centilitres, and Option C converts litres to millilitres instead.

questions.question: A winery produced 30,000 litres of wine at N1,500 per litre ex-factory. Assume excise on wine is N0.65 per litre plus 20% ad valorem. What is the excise duty?
questions.explanation: Specific: 30,000 x N0.65 = N19,500; ad valorem: 30,000 x N1,500 x 20% = N9,000,000; total N9,019,500. Option D uses 30% instead of 20%, and Option C uses the N1.50 spirits rate per litre.

questions.question: A cigar maker's ex-factory sales of other tobacco products are N18,000,000. Assume excise on other tobacco is 20% ad valorem with no specific element. What is the excise duty?
questions.explanation: Excise = 20% x N18,000,000 = N3,600,000. Option A uses the spirits ad valorem rate, and Option C applies the VAT rate instead of the excise rate.

questions.question: Assume excise on beer is N0.30 per litre plus 20% of the ex-factory price. If beer sells at N400 per litre ex-factory, what is the excise duty per litre, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Excise per litre = N0.30 + 20% x N400 = N0.30 + N80.00 = N80.30. Option D drops the specific N0.30, and Option C wrongly applies 20% to the price plus the specific duty.

questions.question: Port Harcourt Supplies Ltd paid import duty of N6,000,000 on a consignment. It later re-exported 40% of the consignment unused. Under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 drawback rules, what drawback can it claim?
questions.explanation: Re-exported unused goods earn a 100% drawback of the duty attributable to them: 40% x N6,000,000 = N2,400,000. Option C claims duty on the whole consignment, and Option D uses the share kept in Nigeria.

questions.question: A juice manufacturer paid import duty of N9,000,000 on imported concentrate used to produce 1,000,000 cartons. It exported 300,000 cartons. Under manufacturing drawback (proportionate to imported content in exported goods), what drawback is claimable?
questions.explanation: Drawback = N9,000,000 x 300,000/1,000,000 = N2,700,000. Option D claims all the duty although most output was sold locally, and Option A uses the local-sales proportion.

questions.question: Delta Spirits Ltd imported spirits with a CIF value of $800,000 at $1 = N1,700. The ECOWAS CET rate is 35%. VAT at 7.5% is charged on (CIF + import duty). What is the total of import duty and VAT?
questions.explanation: CIF = 800,000 x 1,700 = N1,360,000,000; duty = 35% = N476,000,000; VAT = 7.5% x N1,836,000,000 = N137,700,000; total N613,700,000. Option B computes VAT on CIF only, and Option D charges VAT only on the duty.

questions.question: Goods with a CIF value of N50,000,000 are imported. Assume the CISS levy is 1% of CIF and the ECOWAS levy is 0.5% of CIF. What is the combined CISS and ECOWAS levy?
questions.explanation: CISS N500,000 + ECOWAS N250,000 = 1.5% x N50,000,000 = N750,000. Options A and D give only one of the two levies, and Option C treats 1.5% as 15%.

questions.question: A brewery produced 1,000,000 litres of beer at N600 per litre ex-factory. Assume excise is N0.30 per litre plus 20% ad valorem, charged on all litres produced. Separately, 250,000 litres were exported and import duty of N4,000,000 was paid on the imported inputs used in the exported beer only. What is the excise duty?
questions.explanation: Excise = 1,000,000 x N0.30 + 1,000,000 x N600 x 20% = N300,000 + N120,000,000 = N120,300,000. Option A wrongly nets off the import duty drawback, which is a refund of customs duty and not a deduction from excise, and Option C reduces the base although the stem states excise applies to all litres produced.

questions.question: Medical equipment with a CIF value of N20,000,000 attracts import duty at the 5% CET band. VAT at 7.5% is charged on CIF plus duty. What is the VAT base on importation?
questions.explanation: VAT base = CIF + import duty = N20,000,000 + N1,000,000 = N21,000,000. Option A omits the duty, Option C is the VAT itself (7.5% of the base), and Option B wrongly adds the VAT into its own base.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the repealed Companies Income Tax Act regime, failure to deduct tax attracted a penalty of 10% of the amount not deducted, plus interest. How does the penalty for failure to deduct under section 105 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 compare?

options.a: It has been reduced to 5% of the amount not deducted
options.b: It is unchanged at 10% of the amount not deducted
options.c: It is now 20% of the amount not deducted, double the old rate
options.d: It is now 40% of the amount not deducted, four times the old rate

questions.explanation: The NTAA 2025 raised the penalty for failure to deduct from 10% to 40% of the amount not deducted, quadrupling it to push payers to comply. Option B is tempting because 10% still appears in the new law, but only as the per annum penalty for failure to remit. Options A and C are not the new rate.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the repealed VAT Act, VAT revenue was shared 15% to the Federal Government, 50% to States and FCT and 35% to Local Governments. What change does section 81(1) of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 make?

options.a: Local Governments rise to 55% and States and FCT fall to 35%
options.b: There is no change; the old ratio is carried over
options.c: The Federal Government share rises to 85% and States fall to 15%
options.d: The Federal Government share falls to 10% and the States and FCT share rises to 55%, while Local Governments stay at 35%

questions.explanation: Under the NTAA 2025 the Federal Government gives up 5 percentage points to the States and FCT, moving from 15/50/35 to 10/55/35, while Local Governments keep 35%. Option C moves revenue in the wrong direction. Option A swaps the States and Local Government shares, and option B ignores the reform.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the old Finance Act regime, the N50 electronic money transfer levy on electronic receipts of N10,000 or more was borne by the recipient. Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 (from 1 January 2026), who bears the N50 stamp duty on an electronic transfer of N10,000 or more?

options.d: The bank, from its own income

questions.explanation: From 1 January 2026 the N50 duty on transfers of N10,000 or more is charged to the person making the transfer, so banks now deduct it from the sender's account. Option A describes the old electronic money transfer levy. Options D and C are not how the duty is charged.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: From what date did the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 commence?
questions.explanation: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 was assented to on 26 June 2025 but commenced on 1 January 2026. Option D is the assent date, not the commencement date, and the other options are not dates fixed by the Act.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: On what date was the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 assented to by the President?
questions.explanation: The President signed the four reform Acts on 26 June 2025; the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 then took effect from 1 January 2026. Option D is the commencement date, which students often confuse with the assent date.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Which of the following laws was NOT repealed by the Nigeria Tax Act 2025?
questions.explanation: Customs duty was left outside the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and remains under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023. Options A, C and D were all repealed and their substance consolidated into the Nigeria Tax Act 2025.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Which of the following Acts was repealed by the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 with effect from its commencement?

options.a: The Tertiary Education Trust Fund (Establishment) Act
options.b: The Nigeria Export Processing Zones Act

questions.explanation: The Petroleum Profits Tax Act is one of the twelve enactments listed as repealed by the Nigeria Tax Act 2025. Option D still governs customs, while Options A and B were amended rather than repealed.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: After the 2025 reforms, where are the main rules on Value Added Tax in Nigeria found?

options.a: In the Value Added Tax Act, which continues alongside the new Acts
options.b: In the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, after the repeal of the Value Added Tax Act
options.c: In the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023
options.d: In the Joint Revenue Board (Establishment) Act 2025

questions.explanation: The Value Added Tax Act was repealed and VAT now sits in the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 as one chapter of a consolidated statute. Option A is wrong because the old Act no longer operates, and Option D concerns the inter-governmental revenue board, not the VAT charge.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Stamp duties in Nigeria were previously governed by the Stamp Duties Act. After the 2025 reforms, they are governed by:

options.a: The Stamp Duties Act, as amended in 2025

questions.explanation: The Stamp Duties Act was repealed and its provisions were absorbed into the Nigeria Tax Act 2025. Option A is wrong because the old Act was repealed rather than amended, and Option D only establishes the revenue authority.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Which old law, repealed by the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, provided the Pioneer Status Incentive now replaced by the Economic Development Tax Incentive?

options.b: The Industrial Development (Income Tax Relief) Act

questions.explanation: Pioneer status was granted under the Industrial Development (Income Tax Relief) Act; that Act was repealed and the Economic Development Tax Incentive took its place. Options A, C and D were also repealed, but none of them was where pioneer status came from.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Which Act did the Nigeria Revenue Service (Establishment) Act 2025 repeal?

options.d: The Federal Inland Revenue Service (Establishment) Act 2007

questions.explanation: The Nigeria Revenue Service (Establishment) Act 2025 repealed the FIRS (Establishment) Act 2007 and replaced the FIRS with the Nigeria Revenue Service. Options A and C were repealed by the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, not by the establishment Act.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: A company's old correspondence refers to the 'FIRS'. Under the 2025 reform Acts, which body now performs that role?

options.a: The State Internal Revenue Service of each state

questions.explanation: The FIRS was restructured and renamed the Nigeria Revenue Service by the Nigeria Revenue Service (Establishment) Act 2025. Option D coordinates federal and state tax administration rather than collecting federal taxes, and Option B handles customs.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the 2025 reform Acts, the Joint Tax Board (JTB) has been replaced by:

options.c: The Office of the Tax Ombud

questions.explanation: The Joint Revenue Board (Establishment) Act 2025 replaces the JTB with the Joint Revenue Board, which harmonises and coordinates revenue administration across governments. Option B is the successor of the FIRS, and Options A and C are separate bodies under the same Act.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: The Joint Revenue Board (Establishment) Act 2025 created an independent office to review taxpayers' complaints about taxes, levies, fees, customs duty and excise matters. What is it called?

options.d: The Office of the Tax Ombud

questions.explanation: The Office of the Tax Ombud is an impartial complaints reviewer created by the Joint Revenue Board (Establishment) Act 2025. Option B hears formal tax appeals rather than complaints, and Option A is the collecting authority whose conduct may be complained about.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 repealed the Taxes and Levies (Approved List for Collection) Act. What was that Act's main role?

options.a: It listed the taxes and levies that each tier of government could collect
options.b: It established the Federal Inland Revenue Service as an agency
options.c: It imposed customs duty on goods imported into Nigeria
options.d: It fixed the standard rate of VAT for all supplies

questions.explanation: The Approved List Act set out which taxes and levies the federal, state and local governments could collect; its repeal removed, for example, state authority to collect certain business premises fees and development levies under it. Options B, C and D describe customs, VAT and FIRS laws instead.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: How did the standard VAT rate change when VAT moved from the old Value Added Tax Act (as amended by the Finance Act 2019) into the Nigeria Tax Act 2025?
questions.explanation: The standard rate was 7.5% under the Finance Act 2019 amendment and remains 7.5% under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025. Option A describes the 2019 change from 5% to 7.5%, which happened before the 2025 reforms.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the old Value Added Tax Act, the Federal Government took 15% of VAT revenue. What is the Federal Government's share under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025?
questions.explanation: The Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 sets VAT sharing at 10% Federal, 55% States and FCT, and 35% Local Governments, so the federal share fell from 15% to 10%. Option C is the new state share, and Option A is not a VAT share under either system.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Suppose distributable VAT revenue for a period is N600,000,000,000. Under the old Value Added Tax Act the States' share was 50%; under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 it is 55% (States and FCT). By how much does the States' share increase?
questions.explanation: New share 55% x N600,000,000,000 = N330,000,000,000; old share 50% = N300,000,000,000; increase = 5% x N600,000,000,000 = N30,000,000,000. Option C gives the new share itself rather than the increase.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, what is the rate of the development levy, and on what base is it charged?

options.a: 3% of total profits after capital allowances

questions.explanation: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 imposes a development levy of 4% on the assessable profits of companies chargeable to tax. Option D is lower than the statutory rate, and Option C uses turnover, which is not the base.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 development levy consolidated several earmarked levies. Which of the following was NOT replaced by it?

options.b: The Nigeria Police Trust Fund levy

questions.explanation: The 4% development levy replaced earmarked company levies such as the tertiary education tax, the NITDA levy, the NASENI levy and the Police Trust Fund levy. VAT is a separate consumption tax that continues under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, so it was not replaced.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Which companies are excluded from the development levy under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025?

options.c: All companies with losses brought forward
options.d: Companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange

questions.explanation: The levy applies to all companies chargeable to tax other than small companies and non-resident companies. Options B and D are not exempt categories, and Option C confuses the levy base with relief for losses.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Ilorin Cement Ltd (not a small company) has assessable profits of N250,000,000. Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, the development levy is 4% of assessable profits, and 50% of the levy goes to the Tertiary Education Trust Fund. How much of the company's levy goes to the Tertiary Education Trust Fund?
questions.explanation: Levy = 4% x N250,000,000 = N10,000,000; TETFund share = 50% x N10,000,000 = N5,000,000. Option C is the whole levy, and Option D uses the old idea of a 2% education tax.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Total development levy collected in a month under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 is N40,000,000. The Nigerian Education Loan Fund receives 15% and the National Cybersecurity Fund receives 5%. What is their combined share?
questions.explanation: Combined share = (15% + 5%) x N40,000,000 = 20% x N40,000,000 = N8,000,000. Option C includes only the education loan share, and Option A is the TETFund share.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, what is the companies income tax rate for a small company?
questions.explanation: Small companies are taxed at 0% under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, while other companies pay 30%. Option C is the rate for companies that are not small, and Option D confuses the minimum effective tax rate with the small company rate.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Ondo Logistics Ltd has annual gross turnover of N90 million and total fixed assets of N180 million. It provides haulage (not professional) services. Under the 2025 Acts, how is it classified?

options.a: A small company, since turnover is not more than N100 million and fixed assets are not more than N250 million
options.b: Not a small company, since fixed assets exceed N100 million
options.c: A small company only if it also has fewer than 10 employees
options.d: Not a small company, since turnover exceeds N25 million

questions.explanation: A small company under the 2025 framework has gross turnover of N100 million or less and total fixed assets of N250 million or less, with professional service providers excluded. Option D applies the old N25 million threshold, and Option C adds an employee test that the definition does not contain.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Adeyemi & Co Legal Practitioners Ltd has turnover of N60 million and fixed assets of N20 million. Under the 2025 Acts, why is it NOT a small company?

options.a: Because small company status applies only to manufacturing companies
options.b: Because law firms must have fixed assets of at least N250 million
options.c: Because providers of professional services are excluded from the small company definition
options.d: Because its turnover exceeds N50 million

questions.explanation: Even though its turnover and assets are within the limits, a professional service provider such as a law firm is expressly excluded from the small company definition. Option D invents a N50 million limit, and Option A wrongly restricts the relief to manufacturers.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the old Companies Income Tax Act (as amended by the Finance Act 2019), a small company had turnover of not more than N25 million. What is the turnover limit for a small company under the 2025 Acts?
questions.explanation: The 2025 Acts raised the small company turnover limit from N25 million to N100 million, alongside a fixed-asset limit of N250 million. Option B is the fixed-asset limit, not the turnover limit, and Option D is the old figure.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Calabar Holdings Ltd (not a small company) makes a chargeable gain of N40,000,000. Under the old Capital Gains Tax Act the rate was 10%; under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, companies' gains are taxed at 30%. By how much does the tax on this gain increase?
questions.explanation: Old tax 10% x N40,000,000 = N4,000,000; new tax 30% x N40,000,000 = N12,000,000; increase = N8,000,000. Option D is the new tax itself, and Option C is the old tax.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: How does the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 capital allowance regime differ from the old Companies Income Tax Act regime?

options.a: Only buildings now qualify for capital allowances
options.b: The initial allowance is doubled and the annual allowance is abolished
options.c: The initial allowance is abolished and only an annual allowance at fixed class rates on cost is given
options.d: Capital allowances are abolished and depreciation is now deductible

questions.explanation: The old regime gave an initial allowance followed by annual allowances; the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 gives only annual allowances at fixed rates of 10%, 20% or 25% on cost. Option D is wrong because accounting depreciation is still not deductible, and Option A ignores the many other qualifying classes.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Which new charge on goods was introduced by the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 on chargeable fossil fuel products?

options.a: A 5% surcharge based on the retail price
options.b: A 2% stamp duty on fuel receipts
options.c: A 10% customs levy on imported petrol
options.d: A 7.5% excise on crude oil exports

questions.explanation: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 introduced a 5% surcharge on chargeable fossil fuel products, computed on the retail price, with exemptions for items such as cooking gas, kerosene, CNG and renewable energy products. Options B, C and D describe charges that the Act does not create.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the old Value Added Tax Act, input VAT on services and fixed assets generally could not be recovered. How does the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 change this?

options.a: Input VAT on purchases, including services and fixed assets, is recoverable if related to taxable supplies
options.b: Input VAT is recoverable only on goods imported for resale
options.c: Input VAT is recoverable only by small companies below N100 million
options.d: Input VAT is no longer recoverable on any purchase, goods or services

questions.explanation: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 allows input VAT on all purchases, including services and fixed assets, where they relate to taxable supplies, which removes a cost that businesses bore under the old Act. Option D reverses the change, and Option C confuses the small company relief with VAT credit.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, how are exports of services treated for VAT?

options.a: They are zero-rated, so the exporter charges 0% and can recover related input VAT
options.b: They are charged at the standard 7.5% rate
options.c: They are outside VAT and the exporter must deregister
options.d: They are exempt, so related input VAT cannot be recovered

questions.explanation: Exported services are zero-rated under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025: no output VAT is charged and input VAT on related costs can be recovered. Option D describes exemption, which blocks input VAT recovery, and Option B would make exports more expensive.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: For VAT purposes under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 framework, 'goods' are best described as:

options.a: Any supply made for consideration, including services
options.b: Only movable tangible items that can be shipped
options.c: All forms of tangible property, movable or immovable

questions.explanation: Goods for VAT cover all tangible property, whether movable or immovable. Option B wrongly leaves out immovable property, and Option A would include services, which are a separate category of supply.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: A consultancy based in Accra provides online advisory services to Abuja Fintech Ltd, which uses them in Nigeria. Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, is the supply treated as taking place in Nigeria for VAT?

options.a: Yes, because the service is provided to and consumed by a person in Nigeria, wherever it is rendered
options.b: No, because services are never subject to VAT
options.c: Yes, but only if the consultant has an office in Nigeria
options.d: No, because the service was rendered outside Nigeria

questions.explanation: A service is treated as supplied in Nigeria when it is provided to and consumed by a person in Nigeria, regardless of whether it is rendered within or outside Nigeria. Option D looks at where the work is done rather than where it is consumed, and Option C adds a physical-presence test that does not apply.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: A transaction includes both a supply of goods and a supply of a service. How is its VAT classification determined in the goods-and-services framework?

options.a: By the dominant element of the transaction
options.b: Always as a supply of goods
options.c: Always as a supply of services

questions.explanation: For a mixed supply, the dominant element decides whether the transaction is treated as goods or services. Options B and C apply a fixed rule regardless of the facts, and Option D has no basis.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: In comparing how goods and services are taxed in Nigeria, which tax applies to imported goods but has no application to imported services?
questions.explanation: Import duty is charged on goods at CIF value and does not apply to services. VAT in Option A reaches both goods and services, including imported services through non-resident supplier rules.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: How did the old Sales Tax (before VAT was introduced in 1994) differ from VAT under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025?

options.a: Sales tax was multi-stage; VAT is single-stage at the retail point
options.b: Sales tax covered services only; VAT covers goods only
options.c: Sales tax was single-stage at the final point; VAT is multi-stage with input tax credit
options.d: Both are single-stage taxes on retail sales only

questions.explanation: The old sales tax was collected once, at the final retail point, while VAT is charged at each stage, with each business deducting the input VAT it paid. Option A swaps the two, and Option B reverses the scope, since sales tax covered goods only.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: What feature of VAT under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 removes the 'tax on tax' (cascading) effect seen under the old Sales Tax?

options.c: Collection by the Nigeria Revenue Service

questions.explanation: Because each registered business deducts the input VAT it paid from its output VAT, tax is not charged on tax already paid earlier in the chain. Options B, C and D are real features of the VAT system, but none of them stops cascading.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares the scope and administration of the old Sales Tax with VAT under the 2025 Acts?

options.a: Both cover goods only and are administered by the states
options.b: Sales tax covered goods only and was state-administered; VAT covers goods and services and is administered by the Nigeria Revenue Service
options.c: Sales tax covered services only; VAT is administered by the Nigeria Customs Service
options.d: Sales tax covered goods and services and was federally administered; VAT covers goods only

questions.explanation: Sales tax was a state-administered tax on goods, whereas VAT reaches both goods and services and is administered by the Nigeria Revenue Service. Option D reverses the scope, and Option C names the wrong agency.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: A manufacturer sells goods to a wholesaler for N100,000, the wholesaler sells them to a retailer for N150,000, and the retailer sells to a consumer for N200,000 (all VAT-exclusive). With VAT at 7.5% under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and full input VAT credit at each stage, what is the total net VAT remitted along the whole chain?
questions.explanation: Net VAT at each stage is 7.5% of the value added: N7,500 + N3,750 + N3,750 = N15,000, which equals 7.5% of the final price. Option B adds up output VAT without input credit, which is the cascading effect VAT removes, and Option C is only the retailer's net VAT.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: In a month a VAT-registered trader charged output VAT of N3,000,000 and paid input VAT of N1,800,000 on purchases for its taxable supplies. Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 credit mechanism, what net VAT does it remit?
questions.explanation: Net VAT = output VAT - input VAT = N3,000,000 - N1,800,000 = N1,200,000. Option C ignores the input credit, and Option A adds the input VAT instead of deducting it.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Which of these is a new feature of the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 that did not exist under the old Companies Income Tax Act?

options.a: A 30% companies income tax rate for companies that are not small
options.b: A minimum effective tax rate of 15% for large companies and members of multinational groups
options.c: Non-deductibility of capital expenditure in computing profits
options.d: Taxation of company profits by the federal tax authority

questions.explanation: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 introduces a 15% minimum effective tax rate for large companies and constituent entities of multinational groups. Options A, C and D all existed under the old companies income tax regime as well.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, an individual whose annual chargeable income is not more than what amount is exempt from personal income tax?
questions.explanation: Individuals earning N800,000 or less per year are exempt from tax on their income under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025. Option D is the small company turnover limit, not a personal exemption.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the 2025 framework, which agency administers VAT on goods and services, and which administers customs duty on imports?

options.a: VAT: each State Internal Revenue Service; customs duty: the Nigeria Revenue Service
options.b: VAT: the Nigeria Revenue Service; customs duty: the Nigeria Customs Service
options.c: VAT: the Nigeria Customs Service; customs duty: the Nigeria Revenue Service

questions.explanation: VAT is administered by the Nigeria Revenue Service, while customs duty remains with the Nigeria Customs Service under the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023. Option C swaps the agencies, and Option D gives a collecting role to a coordinating board.

questions.topic: Taxation of Goods and Services: Old Law and the 2025 Acts
questions.question: Under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, how are capital gains of companies (other than small companies) taxed?

options.a: At 4% as part of the development levy
options.c: At the companies income tax rate of 30%
options.d: At a flat 10% capital gains tax

questions.explanation: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 aligns the tax on companies' chargeable gains with the 30% companies income tax rate, replacing the old 10% capital gains tax. Option D is the old Capital Gains Tax Act rate, and Option A confuses gains with the development levy.

questions.question: On 1 January 2026, Agbabiaka LLP bought legal research software for N10,000,000 for use in its practice, expecting to use it for 10 years. Under the First Schedule to the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, at what rate is the annual capital allowance on the software claimed?

options.a: 10% of cost each year, over the 10-year expected use
options.b: 50% initial allowance, then 25% of the balance each year

questions.explanation: Software expenditure is in the 25% class with motor vehicles and other capital expenditure, and the allowance is a fixed annual rate on original cost. Option A wrongly follows the firm's own 10-year estimate instead of the statutory rate. Option D is the rate for plant and equipment, and option B is wrong because initial allowances no longer exist.
